meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the August 8, 2019 work session with six members present and Council Member Javiera Caballero on an excused absence (6-0). Council unanimously approved (6-0) the City Manager's priority items adding a presentation by Water Management Director Don Greeley on the city's water back-billing crisis, where Greeley apologized for Automated Meter Reading (AMR) failures and prolonged estimation since summer 2017 and confirmed all back-billing was suspended while staff and the City Attorney evaluate customer relief options. Council also heard a presentation on updating the ~$30 million/year Durham County Transit Plan after light rail's discontinuation (Item 14), gave informal head-nod consensus for localized developer-funded equitable engagement on smaller Beltline proposals (Item 15), and discussed recycling market challenges (Item 12) and fines-and-fees equity grants (Item 6). Council unanimously (6-0) settled the agenda (Consent 1–13; GBA public hearings 16–17).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Excused Absence, and Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the meeting with six members present and Council approved an excused absence for Javiera Caballero (traveling to Charlotte for her child, 6-0). Council also approved the City Manager's priority items (6-0) noting speaker Jennifer Johnson would not appear and adding a presentation on water back-billing.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Citizens Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Items 1–17, asking about rising per-mile sidewalk construction costs (Item 7), praising the Meet Me at the Park grant advancing an unfunded Participatory Budgeting project (Item 11), and pulling Item 6 (fines/fees equity grant) and Item 12 (recycling ILA). During public comment, Mr. Friedman criticized Council's budget vote against Chief Davis's police patrol staffing request and urged dropping the 'Durham for All' slogan; Chris Tiffany also spoke.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items (Fines and Fees Grant; Solid Waste Recycling Market Update)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained exploratory work with the Center for Advanced Hindsight under the National League of Cities fines-and-fees equity grant (Item 6), and Solid Waste Director Jim Reiber briefed Council on changing global recycling markets (Item 12).

agenda_items.title: Durham County Transit Plan Proposed Approach and Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning and Transportation staff outlined the approach for redirecting roughly $30 million per year in County transit tax revenue after light rail's discontinuation, coordinating with GoTriangle and the MPO to define partner roles and fund staff support without City general revenue.

agenda_items.title: Urban Avenue Street Closure and Localized Equitable Engagement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council gave informal head-nod direction empowering administration to conduct localized, potentially developer-financed neighborhood engagement on smaller Beltline-related projects rather than waiting for the citywide Equitable Engagement Plan, subject to Council review when the project returns.

agenda_items.title: Water Back-Billing Presentation and Customer Relief Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management Director Don Greeley explained that staffing/protocol lapses since summer 2017 allowed failed drive-by Automated Meter Reading (AMR) meters to remain in estimated billing, resulting in large catch-up bills. All back-billing was suspended while staff and the City Attorney prepare field repairs and legal/equitable relief options within 1–2 months; Council members weighed legal limits on selective discounts against forgiving surprise back-bills or offering friendly payment terms.

agenda_items.title: Board Ballot and Settling the Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following DeDreana Freeman's fourth vote confirming Ms. Balakwa's nomination, Council voted 6-0 to settle the agenda with Consent items 1 through 13 and GBA public hearing items 16 and 17.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero
votes.discussion_detail: Approved excused absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero while picking up her child in Charlotte.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Item 19 Removal; Water Back-Billing Presentation)
votes.discussion_detail: Removed Citizen Matter Item 19 (Jennifer Johnson) and added Don Greeley's presentation on water back-billing.

meetings.title: Durham City Council August 5, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Returning from summer recess on August 5, 2019 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council recognized Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness Month, Love and Respect Ministry, the Hillside Park Basketball Courts award, National Night Out, and the Algonquin Tennis Club state historical marker before confirming Earl Bradley to the Workers' Rights Commission and adopting the Consent Agenda 7-0. In two consecutive quasi-judicial hearings, Council voted 7-0 to grant Major Special Use Permit M1900001 (with a signalization coordination condition) and Site Plan D1800303 for a 105,000-square-foot North Carolina Central University Student Center—after neighbors raised notice and parking concerns—and 7-0 to approve MSUP M1900002 and Site Plan D1800032 for a ready-mix concrete plant at 1435 Camden Avenue. Council then unanimously passed 7-0 across all motions for East Carver Street right-of-way annexation (Item 34), Mist Lake Drive permanent street closing and access easement (Item 35), Cardinal Oaks annexation (Item 36), the landmark Patterson Place Compact Suburban Design District text amendment, rezoning, and street network (Item 37, following a compromise protecting New Hope Creek and prohibiting payday lenders), and service area fees for the Andrews Chapel lift station (Item 38) and Copley Farm sewer outfall (Item 39).

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Hillside Park Award, and Workers' Rights Commission Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the post-recess meeting to order with all seven members present. Council presented proclamations for Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness Month (with Duke's Dr. Jeffrey Marcus), Love and Respect Ministry (Dennis Garrett), National Night Out, and the Algonquin Tennis Club's upcoming state historical marker, plus the APA-NC Great Places People's Choice Award for Hillside Park Basketball Courts. Council approved the City Clerk's priority appointment of Earl Bradley to the Workers' Rights Commission 7-0 and swore him in.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the Consent Agenda covering minutes, Workers' Rights Commission appointment, June 2019 travel performance audit, GARE Welcome Home grant, NCDOT and FTA transit planning grants, Bloomberg Mayor's Challenge agreement with Duke, MPO web applications, NC 54 sidewalk and Safe Routes to School agreements, water supply property ordinance, Triangle Water Supply Partnership, Flowers Drive sewer transfer, May/June bid reports, and municipal software contracts. Council adopted the Consent Agenda unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Hearing — NCCU Student Center (MSUP M1900001 & Major Site Plan D1800303)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Eliza Monroe presented North Carolina Central University's request for a Major Special Use Permit and Major Site Plan to construct a 2.5-story, 105,000-sq-ft student center replacing a 228-space parking lot with 110 spaces on campus. Nearby residents Reinhard Kelly, Charles Kelly, Ronald McCoy, and Jillian Riley testified about short quasi-judicial notice, student overflow parking on Cecil Street, and event traffic, urging a delay, while NCCU counsel Bill Bryan and witnesses defended UDO parking compliance and campus transit plans. Council added a staff-endorsed signalization coordination condition, asked staff to review notice periods and facilitate neighbor-university talks, and approved MSUP M1900001 and Site Plan D1800303 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Hearing — 1435 Camden Avenue Concrete Manufacturing Plant (MSUP M1900002 & Site Plan D1800032)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Danny Cultra presented WJD Holdings LLC and Raleigh Concrete LLC's application for a ready-mix concrete plant on 10.058 industrial acres at 1435 Camden Avenue, noting the Board of Adjustment previously granted variances from the 1,500-foot residential separation and major-thoroughfare access rules (B180008) because nearby residential parcels lie in floodway and Camden Avenue already carries industrial traffic. Property owner Dan Wall, plant manager Tim Brown, engineer Dan Papst, traffic engineer, and appraiser Jarvis Martin testified on impervious surface reduction (74% to ~70%), stormwater BMPs, Level of Service C traffic, and property values, with no opponents speaking. Council approved MSUP M1900002 and Site Plan D1800032 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation: East Carver Street Right-of-Way
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Jamie Sunyak presented a Public Works voluntary annexation and RS-20 zoning translation for a 10.18-acre portion of East Carver Street right-of-way between Danube Lane and Club Creek Road to enable city roadway maintenance upon completion of the Carver Street extension. With no public speakers, Council approved annexation, consistency statement, and UDO zoning 7-0 across three votes.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Permanent Closing of Mist Lake Drive Portion (1,336 Linear Feet) & Access Easement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jamie Sunyak presented the city's request to permanently close 1,336 linear feet of Mist Lake Drive south of Camden Avenue for the Water Management facility redevelopment at 1600 Mist Lake Drive, paired with a 60-foot access easement for Energy United Propane LLC and BIG Properties LLC. Council approved the street closing order and the road maintenance and access easement 7-0 across two votes.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation: Cardinal Oaks (BDG1900006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Emily Struthers presented Jeff Heath's voluntary annexation and RR / Falls Jordan District B zoning translation for 0.452 acres of Canakeet Drive right-of-way and open space parcels in Cardinal Oaks so the city can assume street maintenance. Council approved annexation, consistency statement, and UDO zoning 7-0 across three votes.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Patterson Place Compact Suburban Design District (Text Amendment, Map Change & Street Network)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Lisa Miller presented the continued Patterson Place Compact Suburban Design District package, highlighting post-May revisions that shrank the core subdistrict per Coalition for Affordable Housing and Transit feedback, prohibited payday lenders district-wide, and secured Beacon Properties' proffered variable Transitional Use Area (TUA) and construction best practices protecting New Hope Creek. DeDreana Freeman questioned density-bonus reliance and lift-station sewer capacity; speakers Mike Waldroop, Dr. Bob Healy (New Hope Creek Corridor Advisory Committee / Sierra Club), attorney Patrick Byker (Beacon Properties), Reynolds Smith (DOST), and John Kent endorsed the compromise. Council passed all five motions—text-amendment consistency, text amendment, map-change consistency, map change, and future street network resolution—unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Andrews Chapel Lift Station Service Area and Fees
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner of Public Works presented an ordinance establishing the associated service area and fees for the Andrews Chapel lift station. With no public comments, Council adopted the ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Copley Farm Sanitary Sewer Outfall Service Area and Fees
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner of Public Works presented an ordinance setting the associated service area and fees for the Copley Farm sanitary sewer outfall. With no questions or public speakers, Council adopted the ordinance 7-0 before adjourning at 1:00 a.m.

votes.item_title: City Clerk's Priority Item — Appoint Earl Bradley to the Workers' Rights Commission
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved the City Clerk's priority appointment of Earl Bradley to the Workers' Rights Commission 7-0, and the Clerk swore him in.

votes.item_title: Item 32 — Grant Major Special Use Permit M1900001 (NCCU Student Center) with Signalization Coordination Condition
votes.discussion_detail: Following testimony from NCCU and Cecil Street neighbors regarding notice and parking, Council granted MSUP M1900001 with staff's recommended conditions plus signalization coordination 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32 — Approve Major Site Plan D1800303 (NCCU Student Center)
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved Major Site Plan D1800303 for the 105,000-sq-ft NCCU Student Center 7-0; staff later confirmed on the record that a transposed open-space/tree-coverage figure appeared only in the staff report and not on the approved site plan.

votes.item_title: Item 33 — Grant Major Special Use Permit M1900002 (1435 Camden Avenue Concrete Manufacturing Plant)
votes.discussion_detail: With no opponents and full expert evidence addressing UDO findings, prior Board of Adjustment variances, traffic, and property values, Council granted MSUP M1900002 by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Item 33 — Approve Major Site Plan D1800032 (1435 Camden Avenue Concrete Manufacturing Plant)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved Major Site Plan D1800032 for the 1435 Camden Avenue concrete plant 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 — Adopt Ordinance Annexing East Carver Street Right-of-Way (10.18 Acres)
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the annexation ordinance for East Carver Street right-of-way 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 — Adopt Consistency Statement for East Carver Street Right-of-Way
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the consistency statement for East Carver Street right-of-way 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 — Adopt Ordinance Amending UDO for East Carver Street Right-of-Way (RS-20)
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the initial RS-20 zoning ordinance for East Carver Street right-of-way 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 35 — Adopt Order Permanently Closing 1,336 Linear Feet of Mist Lake Drive
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the order permanently closing 1,336 linear feet of Mist Lake Drive for the Water Management facility redevelopment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 35 — Authorize City Manager to Enter Road Maintenance and Access Easement (Mist Lake Drive)
votes.discussion_detail: Council authorized the 60-foot road maintenance and access easement with BIG Properties LLC and Energy United Propane LLC 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 36 — Adopt Ordinance Annexing Cardinal Oaks (BDG1900006)
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the annexation ordinance for Cardinal Oaks Canakeet Drive right-of-way and open space parcels 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 36 — Adopt Consistency Statement for Cardinal Oaks

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the July 25, 2019 City Council Work Session, Mayor Steve Schewel presided with five members present and excused absences approved unanimously (5-0) for Jillian Johnson (ill) and DeDreana Freeman (out of town). Schewel presented a Senior Services Ambassador pin to longtime Durham Housing Authority Board member and senior advocate Barbara Lofton. To avoid less favorable indemnification terms under Session Law 2019-92 taking effect August 1, Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items and suspended the rules to approve Item 18 early. Council also referred Item 11 (GoDurham transit advertising policy) back to the City Attorney's Office over First Amendment concerns regarding political and religious speech restrictions, debated water supply protection signage on Item 13, reviewed Item 20's geographic neighborhood engagement model, settled the August 5 agenda, and entered closed session on a mediated claim.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absences, and Senior Services Ambassador Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk called roll with Mayor Steve Schewel and Council Members Vernetta Alston, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece present. Council approved excused absences for Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson (ill) and Council Member DeDreana Freeman (out of town). Mayor Schewel then recognized Barbara Lofton, a 12-year Durham Housing Authority Board member and senior advocate, presenting her with a pin naming her Senior Services Ambassador for the City of Durham.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items (Session Law 2019-92 & Closed Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield and the City Attorney's Office explained that Session Law 2019-92 takes effect August 1, 2019 and would require less favorable indemnification language in construction and professional services contracts if not executed before then. Council Member Charlie Reece noted his usual reluctance to vote at work sessions due to public notice, but supported acting early to prevent project delays. Council unanimously approved the City Attorney's request for a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) on a mediated claim and approved the City Manager's priority items.

agenda_items.title: City of Durham GoTransit Advertising Policy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained that upon policy approval, the city would issue an RFP for a third-party vendor to manage transit advertising on a revenue-sharing basis, referring questionable ads to the department head, City Manager, and City Attorney. Council members raised constitutional concerns about whether prohibiting political and religious speech alongside commercial speech restrictions would pass First Amendment muster. At the City Attorney's request and as clarified by Council Member Javiera Caballero, the item was referred back to staff and the City Attorney's Office for further legal review.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to staff / No vote

agenda_items.title: Ordinance to Regulate Activity on Water Supply Protection Property
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Charlie Reece questioned Water Management staff and Assistant City Attorney Don O'Toole on why the ordinance lists specific prohibited activities such as hunting and fishing in addition to 'no trespassing' signs on city-owned watershed properties in the county. Staff and the attorney's office explained the language was modeled after city park ordinances to provide legal authority to post signs on outlying water protection properties. Another council member asked whether the department could be granted administrative authority over sign wording rather than codifying specific text in an ordinance.

agenda_items.title: Expedited Professional Services Contract (Session Law 2019-92)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A representative from the engineering/surveying firm answered council questions about workforce diversity, reporting approximately 630 employees overall (12% minority employment) and 110 employees in the Raleigh office (11% minority employment), along with recruiting efforts and an acquired surveying firm in Greensboro. Because the contract was affected by the impending August 1 effective date of Session Law 2019-92, Council voted unanimously to suspend the rules and approve Item 18.

agenda_items.title: Geographic-Based Community Engagement Approach
agenda_items.discussion_summary: James Davis of Neighborhood Improvement Services discussed transitioning from project-by-project outreach to a geographic engagement approach using mapping assistance from DataWorks. He confirmed that portions of the Beltline trail converging within a mapped focus area would be covered alongside broader transportation and general service needs for that neighborhood.

agenda_items.title: Board Nomination Report, Settling the Agenda, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced that Council nominated Earl Bradley to the Durham Workers Rights Commission. Council unanimously approved the August 5, 2019 agenda (Consent Items 1-10, 12-17, 19-24, 30, and 31; GBA Public Hearings 32-39) and voted unanimously to enter closed session under the previously read NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) attorney-client consultation language.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a Special Meeting on July 25, 2019 for quasi-judicial procedure training conducted by City Attorney staff ahead of two major special use permits scheduled for public hearing on August 5, 2019 (Item 32 for a proposed student center at North Carolina Central University and Item 33 for a project on Camden Avenue). Staff reviewed the legal distinctions among administrative, legislative, and quasi-judicial decisions, Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Section 5.2 standards, general findings on neighborhood harmony and property values, and review factors such as noise, odor, lighting, and traffic. Presenters emphasized avoiding ex parte communications, swearing in all witnesses, allowing cross-examination, excluding inadmissible hearsay, and relying on competent, substantial expert testimony. Because Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson was ill and Council Member DeDreana Freeman was out of town, attorneys recommended arranging a supplemental briefing for them prior to the August 5 hearing. No votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Training for Upcoming Major Special Use Permits
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney staff briefed Council on quasi-judicial rules governing two major special use permits on the August 5, 2019 agenda (NCCU's proposed student center and a Camden Avenue project). Council members asked questions about UDO Section 5.2, Board of Adjustment and Historic Preservation Commission appeals, ex parte communications, and how evidentiary objections operate when applicants have legal representation and neighboring opponents do not. Staff noted they would prepare procedural scripts for Mayor Steve Schewel and recommended a follow-up session for absent members Jillian Johnson and DeDreana Freeman.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 17, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Convening on June 17, 2019 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council honored Jack Price, Ideal Ortiz, and LGBTQ Pride Month pioneers before voting 7-0 to hire Kimberly Martin Rehberg as City Attorney at a $195,000 salary and approving the Consent Agenda 7-0 (excluding pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23). Following sharp disagreement over Police Chief C.J. Davis's denied request for 18 sworn officers, Council adopted the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget and FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan (including $15.46/hour living wage for part-time workers, Welcome Home, eviction diversion, and an Office of Equity and Inclusion) by a 6-1 split vote—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No after Charlie Reece declined Freeman's friendly amendment for nine officers. On Item 27, Council voted 6-1 on both the bond order and referendum resolution to place a $95 million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond on the November 5, 2019 ballot, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting No. Council concluded by passing pulled Item 9 (Resolution Against White Supremacy, Anti-Semitism, and Islamophobia), Item 13 (HUD lead-based paint grant), Item 20 (Eckerd WIOA youth services), and Item 23 (police psychological testing) unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Tribute to Jack Price, Neighbor Spotlight, Pride Month, and Hiring of City Attorney Kim Rehberg
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel mourned former council member and affordable housing developer Jack Price, presented the Neighbor Spotlight to Ideal Ortiz, and recognized LGBTQ Pride pioneers Mandy Carter and local advocates. Schewel announced that after a 360-degree review, Council voted 7-0 in closed session to hire Interim City Attorney Kimberly Martin Rehberg at $195,000, then held a public 7-0 vote and swore her in.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Priority Items and Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented minor attachment and title updates for Item 9 and Item 11 (Volunteers of America homelessness diversion), which Council accepted 7-0. With Items 9, 13, 20, and 23 pulled for discussion, Council unanimously adopted the remaining Consent Agenda covering appointments, DCLT and Willard Street/Vermillion affordable housing loans, water/wastewater engineering and mutual aid agreements, Public Works Operations Center renovation, Black Wall Street Gardens public art, and WIOA/NCWorks contracts 7-0.

agenda_items.title: FY 2019-20 Budget and FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson introduced the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget and FY 2020-25 CIP, after which Jackie Wagstaff, Pastor Rachel Green, Victoria Peterson, Gloria Washington, and Rev. Jerome Washington urged Council to restore Chief C.J. Davis's 18 requested police officers or Mayor Schewel's nine-officer compromise. After Charlie Reece moved adoption, DeDreana Freeman offered a friendly amendment to add nine officers, which Reece declined under Council's single-motion rule. Mark-Anthony Middleton praised living-wage raises and eviction diversion but voted No to register high-crime neighborhoods' call for police staffing, while Schewel, Reece, Jillian Johnson, Vernetta Alston, Javiera Caballero, and Freeman backed the budget (6-1), citing $650,000 for part-time living wages, $3 million for lowest-paid full-time employees, and non-policing investments.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — $95 Million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond Order and November 5 Referendum
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd presented the $95 million affordable housing G.O. bond order and referendum resolution for the November 5, 2019 ballot, with Mayor Schewel outlining a 1.2-cent average variable tax scenario versus a 1.6-cent fixed rate. Public speakers Brianna Van Belzen, Marie Hill Faison, and former Mayor Wib Gulley backed placing the bond on the ballot while Victoria Peterson demanded written affordability definitions and senior housing details. Vernetta Alston moved adoption, joined in support by Reece, Johnson, Caballero, Schewel, and Middleton, while DeDreana Freeman voted No on both motions (6-1).

agenda_items.title: Resolution Against White Supremacy, Anti-Semitism, and Islamophobia
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Robert DeAngelo, Amy Rosenthal, Josh Ravitch, Deborah Friedman, and Rann Bar-On debated the resolution—some criticizing its framing of foreign terrorism or urging Council to rescind its April 2018 ban on Israeli police exchanges, and Bar-On supporting it while urging condemnation of all local ethno-nationalisms. Author Mark-Anthony Middleton (joined by partner Charlie Reece) defended the resolution as an ongoing moral statement against bigotry while clarifying his 2018 vote targeted militarized policing rather than a boycott, read the full text into the record, and Council passed it 7-0.

agenda_items.title: 2018 U.S. HUD Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction and Healthy Homes Program Grant Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Item 13 to ask whether the over-$3-million HUD lead abatement grant still included local youth job training and which properties were targeted. City Manager Tom Bonfield offered to respond in writing once she provided a working email address, and Council approved the grant ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Contract Amendment with Eckerd Youth Alternatives Inc. (Eckerd Connects) for WIOA Youth Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson asked how many youth the program serves and whether it reaches public housing developments like McDougald Terrace and Oxford Manor. Office of Economic and Workforce Development staffer James Dickens confirmed the federally funded program serves 150 youth countywide across Durham, and Council approved the contract amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Contract for Pre-Employment Psychological Testing Services (Durham Police Department)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Tiffany spoke against placing psychological testing after conditional employment offers, urging deeper background investigations and broader recruiting at NCCU before issuing provisional offers. Council approved executing the pre-employment psychological testing contract 7-0.

votes.item_title: Hire Kimberly Martin Rehberg as City Attorney at $195,000 Annual Salary
votes.discussion_detail: Following a closed-session 360-degree evaluation and unanimous selection, Council voted 7-0 in open session to hire 15-year city litigator and Interim City Attorney Kimberly Martin Rehberg at a $195,000 salary, and the City Clerk administered her oath of office.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Updates to Item 9 and Item 11)
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously accepted the City Manager's minor title/attachment updates to Item 9 and Item 11 by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-8, 10-12, 14-19, 21-22, 24-25, 35, excluding pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23)
votes.discussion_detail: Excluding pulled Items 9, 13, 20, and 23, Council unanimously adopted the Consent Agenda 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt FY 2019-20 Annual Budget, FY 2020-25 Capital Improvement Plan, and Related Ordinances
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton clarified on the record that closed-caption graphics briefly obscured his vote display.
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved adoption of the $476 million budget without the Police Chief's requested 18 new sworn officers (declining DeDreana Freeman's friendly amendment to add 9 officers). Council approved the budget 6-1, with Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No to protest the omission of new police positions for high-crime communities despite supporting the budget's wage and housing investments.

votes.item_title: Item 27 — Adopt Bond Order Authorizing Issuance of Not More Than $95 Million in Affordable Housing General Obligation Bonds
votes.discussion_detail: Vernetta Alston moved adoption of the $95 million affordable housing G.O. bond order after public hearing testimony and finance scenarios from David Boyd and Mayor Schewel; the motion passed 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

votes.item_title: Item 27 — Adopt Resolution Setting Special Bond Referendum on $95 Million Affordable Housing Bond for November 5, 2019 Ballot
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the companion resolution placing the $95 million affordable housing bond referendum on the November 5, 2019 ballot 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

votes.item_title: Item 9 — Adopt Resolution Against White Supremacy, Anti-Semitism, and Islamophobia
votes.discussion_detail: After five public speakers debated the resolution's language and the Council's April 2018 police-exchange resolution, author Mark-Anthony Middleton read the text into the record and Council unanimously adopted the resolution 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13 — Adopt Grant Project Ordinance for 2018 U.S. HUD Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction and Healthy Homes Program Grant
votes.discussion_detail: Following questions from Victoria Peterson regarding job training and targeted housing sites, Council adopted the HUD lead-hazard grant project ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20 — Authorize City Manager to Execute Contract Amendment with Eckerd Youth Alternatives Inc. (Eckerd Connects) for WIOA Youth Services
votes.discussion_detail: After James Dickens confirmed the federal WIOA contract serves 150 youth countywide, Council approved the contract amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 23 — Authorize Execution of Contract for Police Pre-Employment Psychological Testing Services
votes.discussion_detail: Following public comment by Chris Tiffany urging stronger pre-offer background checks, Council unanimously authorized the pre-employment psychological testing contract 7-0.

disagreements.issue: Police Officer Staffing (18 or 9 Sworn Officers) vs. Living Wage and Non-Policing Priorities in FY 2019-20 Budget
disagreements.summary: Council divided over excluding Police Chief C.J. Davis's request for 18 new sworn officers (and declining a 9-officer compromise) in favor of funding living wages for part-time city employees and equity/housing programs without raising property taxes, passing the budget 6-1.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the $476 million FY 2019-20 budget without adding 18 new sworn police officers, prioritizing a $15.46/hour living wage for part-time staff, low-wage full-time raises, eviction diversion, and housing/equity programs without a property tax hike.
side_a_arguments: With limited revenue tools outside property taxes that burden low-income and older homeowners, funding both 18 new officers and part-time living wages was not feasible without raising taxes.

The $60 million police budget already absorbs 15 grant-funded sworn positions and adds two latent print examiners; resources are urgently needed for living wages ($650,000), Welcome Home ($200,000), eviction diversion, and the new Office of Equity and Inclusion.

Mayor Schewel noted he had supported a 9-officer compromise for shift relief and training, while DeDreana Freeman offered a friendly amendment for 9 officers (declined by Charlie Reece under single-motion rules) before joining the 6-vote majority.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote No on the budget to protest omitting new patrol officers requested by Chief Davis and residents in high-gun-violence neighborhoods.
side_b_arguments: Over-policing stems from posture and leadership rather than headcount; proactive staffing is what maintains positive safety metrics.

Denying police staffing in high-crime communities like Cornwallis Road, Oxford Manor, and McDougald Terrace reflects a 'pecking order' in progressive politics that ignores vulnerable residents' pleas.
disagreements.resolution: Friendly amendment for 9 officers was declined by mover Charlie Reece; the FY 2019-20 budget and CIP passed 6-1 with Mark-Anthony Middleton voting No.

disagreements.issue: $95 Million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond Order and Referendum (Item 27)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 on both the bond order and referendum resolution to place a $95 million Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond on the November 5, 2019 ballot, with DeDreana Freeman casting the sole No vote.
disagreements.side_a_position: Place the $95 million Affordable Housing Bond on the November 2019 ballot to fund thousands of affordable units, DHA redevelopment, eviction diversion, and homelessness prevention.
side_a_arguments: Routine annual operating funds cannot overcome market-driven gentrification and displacement.
The bond leverages Durham's tax base at an estimated 1.2-cent average variable (or 1.6-cent fixed) tax rate to build lasting nonprofit and Durham Housing Authority capacity.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote No on the $95 million bond order and November referendum resolution.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman recorded No votes on both the bond order and special referendum resolution without delivering floor remarks explaining her dissent (following public comment concerns from Victoria Peterson seeking written affordability definitions and senior housing guarantees).
disagreements.resolution: Both the bond order and referendum resolution passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Preliminary 2019-2020 Budget Work Session - Part 1
meetings.executive_summary: After an initial 9:00 a.m. recess convened by Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson for Mayor Steve Schewel's family medical obligation, all seven council members met at 10:00 a.m. to resolve final contested items in the FY 2019-2020 budget. Following police operational and scheduling discussion with Chief C.J. Davis and a review of part-time livable wage options, Council took three contested show-of-hands votes: a motion to advance the City Manager's budget with $600,000 for part-time livable wages failed; a compromise motion by Mark-Anthony Middleton to fund nine police officers plus the livable wage failed 3-4; and a motion to advance the manager's budget removing the 18 proposed patrol officers while adding $650,000 for the livable wage passed 4-3 (individual hand-vote names were not read into the transcript, though Steve Schewel spoke in favor of the $650,000 livable-wage allocation and Mark-Anthony Middleton advocated adding police officers). Council then debated Mark-Anthony Middleton's proposal to add $335,000 for a three-year ShotSpotter pilot, which Charlie Reece and another member opposed over false-alarm and response-time concerns, before transitioning to the regular afternoon work session without a formal ShotSpotter vote.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, 9:00 a.m. Recess, and Police Operational/Staffing Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson recessed the 9:00 a.m. session until 10:00 a.m. at Mayor Steve Schewel's request; all seven council members attended the 10:00 a.m. session. Police Chief C.J. Davis and staff answered council questions on a proposed operational analysis, beat realignment, 12-hour patrol schedules compared to other departments, officer wellness, and how supplemental staffing covers shift gaps.

agenda_items.title: Part-Time Livable Wage and FY 2019-2020 Budget Motions on Police Positions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council weighed two livable-wage options for part-time employees—raising the wage floor immediately despite compression risks versus spending Q1 classifying positions with $650,000—alongside the manager's proposed 18 police patrol officers. Mark-Anthony Middleton urged funding police capacity based on local crime data rather than abstract principles, while another council member supported Mayor Schewel's proposal without the 18 officers. A motion adding $600,000 for livable wages failed, Middleton's 9-officer compromise failed 3-4, and a motion removing the 18 patrol officers while adding $650,000 for part-time livable wages passed 4-3.

agenda_items.title: ShotSpotter Gunfire Detection Pilot Proposal ($335,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton urged Council to add $335,000 to the FY 2019-2020 budget for a three-year ShotSpotter trial to respond to recurring gunfire in neighborhoods such as Oxford Manor and Cornwallis. Charlie Reece opposed funding ShotSpotter, citing concerns over false alarms and potential harm to priority call response times, and another member echoed unresolved concerns about false alarms and police response protocols. No vote was taken before the special session ended at 1:00 p.m. and transitioned into the regular work session.

votes.notes: Show-of-hands vote ('Motion fails for the three'); individual member names were not read aloud, though Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and spoke in favor of the police addition.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved a compromise to add nine police officers (down from 18) plus part-time livable wage funding; failed on a 3-4 show-of-hands vote.

votes.item_title: Advance City Manager's Budget Removing 18 Patrol Officers and Adding $650,000 for Part-Time Livable Wage
votes.notes: Show-of-hands vote ('Motion passes four to three'); individual member names were not read aloud, though Steve Schewel voiced support for the $650,000 livable-wage plan and an unidentified colleague voiced support for his proposal without the 18 officers.
votes.discussion_detail: Motion to advance the City Manager's budget without funding for 18 additional patrol officers and adding $650,000 for the part-time livable wage over a three-month classification rollout; passed 4-3 by show of hands.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 3, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Convening on June 3, 2019 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council recognized Pride Month on the 50th anniversary of the Stonewall riots and celebrated Participatory Budgeting (PB Durham) exceeding 10,000 voters across three ballots allocating $2.4 million. Council voted 7-0 to approve the City Manager's priority request referring Item 13 (Community Empowerment Fund landlord engagement contract) back to administration for minor contract-language revisions, and reviewed the Consent Agenda with Items 8, 9, and 22 pulled. On a contested annexation ordinance for 1001 Olive Branch Road, Council split 3-4 with Steve Schewel, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting No over sustainability and planning standards, halting the companion rezoning. At the close of the meeting, Council voted 7-0 to authorize an economic development incentive agreement with Famous Chicken Hut Durham, Inc. to help sustain the historic Fayetteville Street restaurant.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Pride Month Proclamation, and Participatory Budgeting Milestone
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m., Council Member Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and the clerk recorded all seven members present. Council presented a Pride Month proclamation marking the 50th anniversary of the Stonewall riots and celebrated PB Durham surpassing its 10,000-voter goal across $2.4 million in community-selected projects.

agenda_items.title: Referral of Item 13 (Community Empowerment Fund Landlord Engagement) Back to Administration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager requested referring Item 13—approving dedicated housing funds for the Community Empowerment Fund for landlord engagement—back to administration due to a minor contract language issue, noting it was expected back at Thursday's work session. Council voted 7-0 to approve the referral.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Items 1–36 and Item 50; Items 8, 9, 13, and 22 Removed)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read Consent Agenda Items 1–36 and Item 50, noting Items 8 (FY18-19 budget amendment), 9 (Racial Equity Task Force initial report), and 22 ($95 million GO bond referendum) were pulled and Item 13 was referred back. Council also briefly noted letterhead formatting on Item 50 (Durham Economic Justice Resolution), while the final consent vote occurred in an omitted portion of the digest.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (consent vote omitted in digest)

agenda_items.title: Annexation and Rezoning for 1001 Olive Branch Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated annexing and rezoning 1001 Olive Branch Road near Research Triangle Park, weighing Planning Commissioners' comments on urban node creation and voluntary affordable housing and school proffers against comprehensive plan and sustainability shortcomings. The annexation ordinance failed 3-4, after which staff confirmed Council did not need to act on the companion rezoning.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Famous Chicken Hut Durham, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Economic development staff (Chris Dickey) presented an incentive agreement to support Famous Chicken Hut at 1319 Fayetteville Street following the passing of matriarch Peggy Tapp and generational transition to her son and cousin Jeffrey Johnson. Following appreciative remarks from Council and owners, Council voted 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to execute the agreement.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Item Referring Item 13 (Community Empowerment Fund Contract) Back to Administration
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted 7-0 to refer Item 13 back to administration to resolve a minor contract language issue before bringing it to the Thursday work session.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Annexing 1001 Olive Branch Road
votes.notes: Clerk announced Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting no.
votes.discussion_detail: Following debate over RTP-adjacent urban node planning, voluntary affordable housing and school proffers, and sustainability standards, the annexation ordinance failed 3-4. Staff confirmed the companion rezoning did not need to proceed.

votes.item_title: Authorize City Manager to Execute Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Famous Chicken Hut Durham, Inc.
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously authorized an economic development incentive agreement to support structural and continuity needs for the 60-year-old Fayetteville Street restaurant.

disagreements.issue: 1001 Olive Branch Road Annexation and Urban Node Rezoning
disagreements.summary: Council divided 3-4 over whether to annex and rezone 1001 Olive Branch Road near Research Triangle Park, weighing existing comprehensive plan alignment and voluntary proffers against sustainability and growth-management expectations.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support annexation and rezoning as consistent with existing precedent and RTP-adjacent growth.
side_a_arguments: Proximity to Research Triangle Park supports creating an urban node in the area.
The applicant's voluntary proffers for affordable housing and Durham Public Schools followed established precedent.
The proposal met current legal and comprehensive plan standards rather than justifying an ad hoc denial.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny annexation because the project falls short on sustainability and comprehensive plan expectations.
side_b_arguments: Even where current comprehensive plan rules allow it, developers must meet higher sustainability standards.
Approving projects that fail long-term sustainability and generational stewardship principles prevents better development outcomes.
Any urban node in this corridor needs to be planned properly before extending city annexation.
disagreements.resolution: The annexation ordinance failed 3-4, ending consideration of the companion rezoning.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Preliminary 2019-2020 Budget Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: During the May 30, 2019 preliminary FY 2019-2020 budget work session, City-County Planning Director Pat Young presented a status-quo staffing budget funded through prior fee schedule adjustments, highlighting a 92% customer satisfaction rating, an October 2021 statutory deadline for initiating historical zoning enforcement, the Expanding Housing Choices initiative, and staff's decision not to fund a Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay study. Later in the session, staff and the City Attorney's Office reviewed Participatory Budgeting (PB) implementation, audit oversight, and eligibility rules after Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned whether PB should become a de facto funding stream for Durham Public Schools rather than city capital projects. Mayor Steve Schewel concluded by flagging outstanding budget topics for June 6—including police hiring, ShotSpotter, Parks and Recreation part-time pay, eviction diversion, deer management, and Welcome Home—and noting Middleton and Charlie Reece's work on a resolution addressing anti-Semitism, Islamophobia, and white supremacy. No formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: City-County Planning Department FY 2019-2020 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Pat Young and Assistant Director Sara Young reviewed performance outcomes, including 92% customer satisfaction at the Development Services Center, increased zoning violation closures ahead of an October 2021 state statute of limitations deadline, and upcoming Comprehensive Plan and Expanding Housing Choices work. Council members asked about the 1.4% stormwater fund allocation (supporting two floodplain positions) and why a Forest Hills Neighborhood Protection Overlay request was not recommended for funding.

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting (PB) Implementation and Eligibility Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff outlined the upcoming fall PB implementation team, steering committee evaluation, and audit department participation. Mark-Anthony Middleton raised concern about PB becoming a de facto funding stream for Durham Public Schools rather than capital projects and asked how projects are disqualified; staff noted delegate training tensions over capital-project rules, and the City Attorney's office confirmed proposals benefiting private/personal property were disqualified.

agenda_items.title: Summary of Flagged Items for June 6 Budget Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel thanked budget staff and confirmed the list of flagged items for the June 6 budget work session, including police officers, ShotSpotter, part-time pay and Parks and Recreation, eviction diversion, deer management, and Welcome Home. He also noted that Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece would circulate a draft resolution on anti-Semitism, Islamophobia, and white supremacy ahead of the next work session before adjourning at 2:46 p.m.

meetings.executive_summary: In the May 29, 2019 FY 2019-2020 budget work session, Police Chief C.J. Council questioning challenged the 18-officer request by pointing to a 5.58-minute Priority 1 response time—described as a five-year low—and a 15% first-quarter decline in Priority 1 calls for service. Transportation staff reported on Vision Zero, parking operations, upcoming e-scooter launches, and revising the County Transit Plan following cancellation of the light rail project, while Neighborhood Improvement Services covered fair housing and code enforcement. Community Development Director Reginald Johnson closed with affordable housing metrics, J.J. Henderson and Willard Street construction plans, homelessness diversion, and eviction diversion for 200 households, which Mayor Steve Schewel flagged for further review on June 6. No votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department FY 2019-2020 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief C.J. Davis presented the Police Department's budget, proposing 690 FTEs including 18 new patrol officers, two forensic latent print examiners, General Fund absorption of 15 COPS grant positions and the Crisis Intervention Clinician, and expansion of the Community Engagement Unit in public housing. While Davis noted rising firearm-related aggravated assaults in District 2 and a 74% courtesy rating on the ETC survey, council questioning challenged the 18-officer request given five-year-low Priority 1 response times (5.58 minutes) and a 15% drop in Priority 1 calls.

agenda_items.title: Department of Transportation FY 2019-2020 Budget Presentation

agenda_items.title: Department of Community Development FY 2019-2020 Budget Presentation

Henderson / Willard Street apartments, 20% homelessness diversion, and eviction diversion for 200 households, which Mayor Steve Schewel flagged for the June 6 budget session along with police officers, ShotSpotter, and Parks and Rec part-time pay.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, the May 23, 2019 City Council Work Session opened with a demonstration of the chamber's new microphone system and announcements calling for $15/hour part-time worker pay and urgent budget action on gun violence from Mark-Anthony Middleton. Council unanimously approved (7-0) City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority request to suspend the rules and accept Item 33 (a 2019 National Police Athletic League Mentoring Initiative grant) due to a one-week deadline, and pulled Items 7, 17, and 22 during consent review. Finance Director David Boyd reported a projected $4 million-plus positive General Fund budget variance and $15.5 million in excess fund balance alongside parking fund revenue shortfalls, followed by briefings on the 2019 Employee Engagement Survey and a proposed Language Access Plan spearheaded with Council Member Javiera Caballero. Council concluded by hearing board nominations, unanimously approving the upcoming meeting agenda (7-0), and adjourning at 4:08 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Announcements, New Audio System, and 2019 National PAL Mentoring Grant (Item 33)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services demonstrated the upgraded council chamber microphone system, followed by council announcements urging a $15/hour wage for part-time city workers and remarks from Mark-Anthony Middleton calling for short- and long-term gun violence action in the upcoming budget. Council unanimously approved City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority request to suspend the rules and accept Item 33 (the 2019 National Police Athletic League Mentoring Initiative Grant) within its one-week acceptance window, and pulled Items 7, 17, and 22 during consent agenda review.

agenda_items.title: FY 2018-2019 Third Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd reported projections of nearly $5 million in spending savings and over $4 million in positive net General Fund variance despite weaker sales tax collections, leaving fund balance more than $15.5 million above policy minimums. He noted a $1.3 million positive variance in water and sewer, while flagging revenue shortfalls in the parking fund due to garage opening delays, management transition issues, and technology problems.

agenda_items.title: 2019 Employee Engagement Survey Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented results from the 2019 Employee Engagement Survey, showing a six-point increase in day-to-day job satisfaction and an improvement in net engagement from -8 to -6. Presenters recommended recognizing high-scoring managers, requiring action plans from lower-scoring leaders, and expanding leadership development training across city government.

agenda_items.title: Proposed City of Durham Language Access Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Beverly Thompson (Office of Public Affairs) and James Davis (Neighborhood Improvement Services) presented the proposed Language Access Plan, emphasizing culturally competent certified interpretation, rapid phone interpretation services ($0.75/minute for Spanish with ~6-second answer times), and website updates. Council praised Council Member Javiera Caballero for championing the effort and urged identifying top implementation priorities.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations and Settling the Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced nominations to the Citizens Advisory Committee, Durham City-County Appearance Commission, and Durham Cultural Advisory Board (clarifying staggered 2021 and 2022 terms). Council unanimously approved the upcoming meeting agenda including Consent Items and GBA Public Hearings 40-47, and adjourned at 4:08 p.m.

votes.discussion_detail: Approved City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority item requesting suspension of the rules and acceptance of Item 33 (2019 National Police Athletic League Mentoring Initiative Grant Project Ordinance) due to a one-week grant deadline.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 20, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 20, 2019 meeting, the Durham City Council honored former Mayor Wense Grabarek on the anniversary of his 1963 inauguration, proclaimed June 7, 2019 as National Gun Violence Awareness Day with Council Member Vernetta Alston and Moms Demand Action, and reminded residents age 13 and older to vote in Participatory Budgeting. Council pulled Items 14 and 15 from the Consent Agenda, then unanimously passed 7-0 a federal tax-law resolution for Capital Trust Agency Series 2019 revenue bonds, an ordinance aligning stormwater development standards with state law and the city's NPDES permit, and Item 14 adopting FY 2019-20 water and sewer rates. On pulled Item 15 authorizing Local Government Commission (LGC) application and notice resolutions for a $95 million General Obligation bond referendum, Council voted 6-1 to advance the resolutions, with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting No due to timing, fixed-income affordability, and housing authority displacement concerns.

agenda_items.title: Honoring Former Mayor Wense Grabarek, Gun Violence Awareness Proclamation, and PB Durham Reminder
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and guests honored former Mayor Wense Grabarek on the anniversary of his May 20, 1963 inauguration, highlighting his 1963 biracial dialogue and major economic and annexation milestones. Council Member Vernetta Alston read the National Gun Violence Awareness Day proclamation honoring Durham victims, and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton joined a presentation while residents 13+ were urged to vote in PB Durham.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Items 1–28; Items 14 and 15 Pulled)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no priority items from staff, Mayor Schewel read Consent Agenda Items 1–28 covering board appointments, water and street contracts, DPAC audio upgrades, and affordable housing loans. Items 14 (FY19-20 water and sewer rates) and 15 ($95 million GO bond referendum) were pulled for separate action; the consent vote itself was omitted in digest truncation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (consent vote omitted in digest)

agenda_items.title: Capital Trust Agency Tax-Exempt Revenue Bond Series 2019 Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff explained the host-jurisdiction public hearing required under federal tax law for Capital Trust Agency Series 2019 revenue bonds, noting the city carries no repayment obligation or financial impact. No public speakers appeared, and Council voted 7-0 to adopt the resolution.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance Amending Stormwater Performance Standards for Development
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Stormwater staff presented code amendments to align with the city's October 10, 2018 NPDES permit and state session laws that barred local enforcement of Jordan Lake nutrient rules on new development, substituting total suspended solids as a pollutant surrogate while retaining Falls Lake rules. Consultant Tim Savers spoke in support, and Council adopted the ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance Adopting Water and Sewer Rates for FY 2019-20
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following brief staff discussion with Ms. Westbrook on the pulled rate schedule, Council voted 7-0 to adopt the ordinance setting FY 2019-20 water and sewer service rates.

agenda_items.title: $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum Resolutions (LGC Application and Notice of Intent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman voiced discomfort moving the $95 million GO bond referendum forward immediately alongside other cost increases without clear protections for fixed-income residents, an economic development plan, or safeguards against housing authority displacement. Council voted 6-1 to adopt the LGC application, notice of intent, and statements-of-fact resolutions.

votes.discussion_detail: Council approved the federal tax-law host resolution with no city financial obligation.

votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted stormwater code revisions aligning local standards with the city's federal NPDES permit and North Carolina session laws on Jordan Lake.

votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the FY 2019-20 water and sewer rate ordinance after pulling Item 14 from consent.

votes.item_title: Adopt Resolutions for Notice of Intent, LGC Application, and Statements of Fact for $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum (Item 15)
votes.notes: Audio ASR rendered 'Council Member Freeman voting no' as 'the item of agreement voting no'.
votes.discussion_detail: Council adopted the three required procedural resolutions to apply to the Local Government Commission for the $95 million GO bond referendum, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over timing and displacement concerns.

disagreements.issue: Timing and Displacement Risks of $95 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum (Item 15)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to advance procedural Local Government Commission filings for the $95 million General Obligation bond referendum, with DeDreana Freeman urging a one-year delay to protect fixed-income and public-housing residents.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance the $95 million GO bond LGC filings on the current schedule.
side_a_arguments: Proceeding with notice of intent and LGC application keeps the $95 million bond referendum on track for the current cycle.
The bond package reflects figures outlined in the Mayor's letter to Council.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the $95 million bond referendum until the next cycle pending anti-displacement and tax-relief measures.
side_b_arguments: Advancing the bond alongside other cost and rate increases creates financial strain for fixed-income residents without clear relief levers.
An economic development plan should be established before moving forward.
Federal housing authority desegregation pushes are driving displacement of predominantly African-American housing authority residents.
disagreements.resolution: Resolutions passed 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting no.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 9, 2019 City Council Work Session, Council approved an excused absence for Javiera Caballero, gave consensus for an upcoming economic justice resolution on state worker legislation, and heard Mark-Anthony Middleton's update on drafting a resolution against anti-Semitism, Islamophobia, and white supremacy with Charlie Reece. Council unanimously approved the City Manager's and City Attorney's priority items (including a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) on a mediated claim) and reviewed consent items including a $95 million GO bond referendum, water/sewer rates, commercial organics recycling, and tie-breaking rules for Workers Rights Commission terms. Downtown Durham, Inc. and Office of Economic and Workforce Development staff presented the FY 2018-2019 Municipal Service District annual report highlighting ambassador response near the downtown gas explosion, retail initiatives, public space art activations, and panhandling outreach. Council concluded by receiving board nominations (breaking an at-large tie for Grace Castle on the Mayor's Council for Women), settling the agenda (Consent 1-28, GBA Item 31, Public Hearings 32-33), and entering closed session.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously granted an excused absence to Javiera Caballero; Mark-Anthony Middleton noted DeDreana Freeman would arrive late and asked him to pull placeholder items. Members gave thumbs-up consent for a future economic justice resolution on state worker legislation, and Middleton reported that he and Charlie Reece were consulting stakeholders to draft a model resolution against anti-Semitism, Islamophobia, and white supremacy. Council also discussed scheduling a partner funding presentation after May 23 to avoid overloading that agenda alongside the Language Access Plan and Racial Equity Task Force.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield noted that Item 36 speaker Molly Stillman would not appear, and Council unanimously approved the manager's priority item. The City Attorney's Office requested a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation on a presented claim and requested mediation, which Council approved unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Workers Rights Commission Term-Allocation Method
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During consent review, Council discussed using a lottery draw by the City Clerk to assign two-year versus one-year initial terms when Workers Rights Commission nominees tied in votes. Items pulled for discussion included Item 8, materials testing contracts (Items 12/13), and Item 15 ($95 million general obligation bond referendum), while a member requested an email explanation of commercial organics recycling under Item 28.

agenda_items.title: FY 2018-2019 Downtown Durham Municipal Service District (MSD) Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Summer Alston (OEWD) and Nicole Thompson (Downtown Durham, Inc.) presented the MSD annual report, noting Downtown Ambassadors' storm cleanup and proximity to the recent downtown gas explosion, the Shop Second Saturday retail initiative, local artist activations in Five Points, panhandling outreach research, pop-up retail spaces, and M/WBE small business assistance.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations, Settling the Agenda, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced 13 nominees to the Workers Rights Commission, nominations to the Mayor's Council for Women (with a vote change breaking a tie in favor of Grace Castle), and nominees to the Planning Commission, Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission, and Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee. Council unanimously approved the regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-28, GBA Item 31, and GBA Public Hearings 32-33) and entered closed session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 6, 2019
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting on May 6, 2019, the Durham City Council recognized local and state student contest winners, heard a Sesquicentennial history moment on Chief Justice Earl Warren and Brown v. Board of Education, and passed the Consent Agenda 7-0 (including a resolution supporting the Mental Health Protection Act, Equality for All Act, and full HB2 repeal) after pulling Item 6 for speakers. Under General Business, Council appointed Darren Chester as an at-large alternate to the Housing Appeals Board by ballot and received the 2018-19 Durham Youth Commission Annual Report. At the end of the lengthy session, Council held an extended discussion on pulled Item 6—a resolution honoring the life of El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz (Malcolm X) championed by DeDreana Freeman—addressing community concerns over anti-Semitism and anti-Islamophobia, unanimously passing the revised resolution 7-0 while tasking Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece with drafting a companion resolution against anti-Semitism and Islamophobia by June 6.

agenda_items.title: Student Contest Recognition, Brown v. Board History Moment, and Spirit Airlines Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council recognized Durham students across K-2, 3-5, and 6-8 divisions who won local and state honors, followed by a Sesquicentennial history presentation detailing Chief Justice Earl Warren's effort to secure a unanimous Supreme Court opinion in Brown v. Board of Education. An announcement also noted seven new direct Spirit Airlines flights.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 2–33, Excluding Pulled Item 6)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved Consent Agenda Items 2–33 unanimously 7-0, including annual board reports, the FY20 Planning Work Program, homelessness HMIS/coordinated entry funding with NCCEH, $263 million water and sewer BAN application, 203 South Gregson Street condemnation, and a resolution supporting the Mental Health Protection Act, Equality for All Act, and full HB2 repeal. Item 6 was pulled for speakers.

agenda_items.title: Housing Appeals Board Appointment and 2018-19 Durham Youth Commission Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: By written ballot on the General Business Agenda, Council appointed Darren Chester as an at-large alternate on the Housing Appeals Board as Mr. Green moved into a regular seat. Elise Frazier, Youth Initiative Analyst, then began presenting Item 23, the 2018-19 Durham Youth Commission Annual Report.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Appointed Darren Chester by ballot; Item 23 Informational

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Recognition of the Life of El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz (Malcolm X)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed work-session revisions and community concerns regarding anti-Semitism and anti-Islamophobia surrounding DeDreana Freeman's resolution honoring Malcolm X and its relevance to reentry advocates. Council passed the resolution 7-0, Mayor Schewel read it into the record for Local Reentry Council representative Ben Haas, and Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece agreed to draft a companion resolution condemning anti-Semitism and Islamophobia by June 6.

votes.item_title: Adopt Resolution in Recognition of the Life of El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz (Malcolm X) (Item 6)
votes.notes: Council also asked Mark-Anthony Middleton and Charlie Reece to draft a resolution against anti-Semitism and Islamophobia by the June 6 work session.
votes.discussion_detail: After extensive reflection by Council Members Freeman, Reece, and Middleton on finding common ground and opposing both anti-Semitism and anti-Islamophobia, Council unanimously adopted the resolution.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the April 18, 2019 City Council Work Session, Mayor Steve Schewel presided with Charlie Reece on an excused absence. Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items and the City Attorney's closed-session request covering four pending litigation matters, then voted unanimously to suspend the rules and pass Item 21 (a resolution supporting the 2020 Census, moved by Mark-Anthony Middleton). During Citizens Matters, residents addressed police complaint handling and a formerly incarcerated baker's $3 million expansion request, with Mayor Schewel later clarifying that city funding flows through competitive processes rather than direct individual allocations. Council also reviewed Item 19's proposed $263 million water and sewer bond anticipation notes, heard a presentation on three design options for the Downtown Durham Wayfinding Program (Item 24), received Housing Appeals Board nominations, settled the upcoming agenda, and entered closed session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Attorney Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield introduced replacement text for Item 6 (Malcolm X recognition resolution), supplemental Items 32 (Participatory Budgeting update) and 33 (Mental Health Protection Act, Equality for All Act, and repeal of HB 142—later noted as HB 2 in heading), and expedited consideration of Item 21 (2020 Census resolution). The City Attorney requested closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding four lawsuits (including Lidna v. City of Durham/C.J. Davis, Friedman, NC Coalition for Israel, and Gunter). Both priority packages passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Support of the 2020 Census
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Because of compressed coordination timelines for the Durham area 2020 Census cohort, Council voted unanimously to suspend the rules during the work session. Following a motion by Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council unanimously adopted the 2020 Census support resolution.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters (Police Complaints and Re-Entry Bakery Proposal)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Tiffany read excerpts regarding police complaint handling and discrimination reporting, and Kiwanah Hester requested $3 million in support to expand a bakery and culinary training facility for formerly incarcerated individuals. Later in the meeting, Mayor Steve Schewel explained that Council avoids direct individual budget earmarks and encouraged Hester to pursue competitive city grant and RFP processes.

agenda_items.title: LGC Application for $263 Million Water and Sewer Bond Anticipation Notes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Treasury Manager briefed Council on applying to the Local Government Commission for up to $263 million in water and sewer revenue bond anticipation notes. She explained that an initial two-to-three-year interest-only interim period aligns borrowing with project spending to avoid premature debt and smooth utility rates prior to a three-to-five-year takeout financing.

agenda_items.title: Housing Appeals Board Nominations, Settling Agenda, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported John Green's nomination to the Housing Appeals Board alongside a tie for the second seat headed to GBA. Council unanimously settled the regular agenda (Consent 2-4, 6-20, 22, 33; GBA Items 1, 23, 25; GBA Public Hearings 26-30), heard a request for an urban tier housing demographics briefing by John Killeen at the next work session, and entered closed session.

agenda_items.title: Downtown Durham Wayfinding Program (TIP C-5605H)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff presented three federally funded (DCHC MPO / NCDOT) wayfinding signage design concepts: Option 1 featuring City of Durham flag colors and branding (favored by nearly 50% of respondents), Option 2 using historic styling, and Option 3 incorporating creative seating kiosks. Staff noted ongoing sign placement programming for major downtown destinations such as City Hall and the library.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Apr 15, 2019 1 of 2
meetings.executive_summary: In Part 1 of the April 15, 2019 Durham City Council meeting, Mayor Steve Schewel opened with extended remarks mourning Kaffenate coffee shop owner Kong Lee and praying for injured victims of the recent downtown Durham gas explosion while praising firefighters, first responders, a PSNC utility worker, and city staff. Council presented the Neighborhood Spotlight award to Creekside at Bethpage volunteer Kevin Walls and heard a History Moment by Eddie Davis and former NC AFL-CIO President James Andrews honoring Durham labor leader Wilbur Hobby. Council Member DeDreana Freeman joined the Week of the Young Child proclamation, Young Male Achievers and mentor Mr. Goff were recognized, and Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton introduced Fire Chief Robert Zoldos for the Sound the Alarm proclamation before Part 2. agenda_items.title: Mayor's Remarks on the Downtown Durham Gas Explosion and Emergency Response

agenda_items.title: Neighborhood Spotlight — Kevin Walls (Creekside at Bethpage)

agenda_items.title: History Moment — Labor Leader Wilbur Hobby
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public historian Eddie Davis and former NC AFL-CIO President James Andrews recounted the career of Durham labor organizer Wilbur Hobby, from cleaning machines at American Tobacco to leading the statewide AFL-CIO, supporting Frank Porter Graham, and advancing worker training and voter registration.

agenda_items.title: Week of the Young Child Proclamation and Young Male Achievers Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel and Council Member DeDreana Freeman presented the Week of the Young Child proclamation thanking city staff partners, followed by recognition of Young Male Achievers and mentor Mr. Goff.

agenda_items.title: Introduction of Sound the Alarm Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton and Fire Chief Robert Zoldos stepped forward to introduce the Sound the Alarm proclamation, which continued at the start of Part 2.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Apr 15, 2019 2 of 2
meetings.executive_summary: Resuming on April 15, 2019 in Part 2, the Durham City Council proclaimed Sound the Alarm Day with Fire Chief Robert Zoldos and unanimously passed the Consent Agenda 7-0, including Item 21 supporting the Medicare for All Act of 2019 (endorsed in public comment by Dr. Heather Kim). Under Item 10 (General Classification and Compensation Plan Recommendations), city workers and union representatives raised concerns over part-time exclusions, supervisor discretion, promotion barriers for Black employees, and a formal meet-and-confer process (with Item 10's final action omitted in digest truncation). Council later voted 7-0 across two motions for a prior zoning map change, voted 7-0 on both the consistency statement and UDO amendment for Item 17 (707 Morehead Avenue townhomes in the Morehead Hill Historic District), and voted 7-0 on Item 18 adopting the FY 2019-20 HUD Annual Action Plan.

agenda_items.title: Sound the Alarm Proclamation and Fire Department Smoke Alarm Campaign

agenda_items.title: Priority Notice and Consent Agenda (Items 1–12 and Item 21 Medicare for All Resolution)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted Attachment 6 was added to Item 10 per work-session questions, and Council passed the Consent Agenda 7-0 including the vacant positions audit, Southeast Region Lift Station contract, Moogfest 2019 agreement, and Item 21 supporting Medicare for All. Dr. Heather Kim then spoke in support of the Medicare for All resolution.

agenda_items.title: General Classification and Compensation Plan Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a staff presentation, speakers including Dante Strebino, Donald Quick, Romi Gaddy, and Sarah Vukalich urged Council to include part-time workers in raising the wage floor, establish systematic meet-and-confer engagement, and curb subjective evaluation and promotion disparities affecting Black employees. Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned staff on implementation; final vote action was omitted in digest truncation.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council resolved a button-pushing issue involving Vernetta Alston to record a 7-0 vote on the consistency statement and voted 7-0 to adopt the UDO amendment ordinance for the preceding zoning map change.
