meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 22, 2018 City Council Work Session (presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel with six members present at roll call and DeDreana Freeman not recorded), Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson introduced a resolution supporting public employee collective bargaining rights and employee organization access—removing Section 4 to resolve prior colleague concerns—alongside UE Local 150 speakers Nathanette Mayo and Dante Strobino requesting departmental meeting access comparable to Governor Cooper's Executive Order 5 and quarterly meetings with the City Manager. After a truncated middle gap, Council wrapped up Participatory Budgeting scheduling and unanimously voted by voice to suspend the rules and approve Item 9 (transcribed as 'item none' in ASR). Staff then presented FY 2018 Dedicated Housing Fund RFP awards (including $327,000 and $750,000 to Durham Community Land Trustees and $175,000 to Housing for New Hope, plus a $2.9 million FY19 DHA recommendation and $2.5 million fall multifamily RFP) and updated Council that Duke University and H.A. Fletcher offered grant funding in lieu of office space on the Jackson Street LIHTC project, enabling a second residential building instead of office space with no extra city subsidy. Council concluded by announcing 13 board/commission appointees and unanimously settling the April 2 meeting agenda by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Support of Public Employee Collective Bargaining Rights and Employee Organizations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson presented a resolution supporting public employee collective bargaining rights and employee organizations—referencing *Janus v. AFSCME Council 31*, Durham's $15/hour minimum wage and paid family leave, and the 50th anniversary of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s Memphis sanitation strike support—after removing Section 4 due to colleague concerns. UE Local 150 statewide president Nathanette Mayo (a 31-year city employee) and organizer Dante Strobino urged restoring prior administrative access rights aligned with Governor Cooper's Executive Order 5, including annual departmental meetings with two weeks' notice and quarterly meetings with City Manager Tom Bonfield.

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting Wrap-Up, Street Parking Inquiry, and Rule-Suspension Approval of Item 9
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming after a middle truncation, Council discussed Participatory Budgeting steering committee project tracking and potential two-year scoping/implementation cycles, briefly questioned an 8-foot parking area from Main Street to Holloway Street, and asked about biosolids drying-pad timelines. Council unanimously approved suspending the rules and adopting Item 9 (garbled in ASR as 'item none') by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: FY 2018 Dedicated Housing Fund RFP Awards Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented informational awards from three December FY18 Dedicated Housing Fund RFPs: under multifamily preservation ($1M available), Durham Community Land Trustees ($327,000) and Housing for New Hope ($175,000); and under neighborhood stabilization ($750,000 available), Durham Community Land Trustees ($750,000), alongside $300,000 for minor home repairs. He explained that Durham Housing Authority (DHA) projects are funded separately—recommending $2.9 million for FY19 via carryover and supplemental funds—and noted plans for a $2.5 million FY19 multifamily RFP in the fall plus an upcoming homelessness RFP.

agenda_items.title: Downtown / Jackson Street LIHTC Project Concept Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff reported that the Phase 1 Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) development team received a perfect site-review score and received an offer from Duke University and H.A. Fletcher to provide grant funding in lieu of occupying commercial office space. This shift allows Phase 1 LIHTC to proceed and sets the stage for a second residential project on the parcel rather than an office building, reducing parking requirements and requiring no additional City subsidy for Phase 1.

agenda_items.title: Appointments and Agenda Settlement for April 2, 2018 Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk read appointment results including Angela Lee, Katie Spencer, Joshua Gunn (7 votes), Zina Howard (5 votes), Tom James (5 votes), Cynthia Penn Hallal (6 votes), and Rachel Wexler (5 votes) among 13 appointees. Council then unanimously settled the April 2 City Council agenda (Consent Items 2–8, 10–15, and Supplemental Item 20; GBA Public Hearing Item 18) by voice vote before adjourning for a City Council photograph.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Mar 19, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton excused absent due to an out-of-state flight mechanical delay, the six present Durham City Council members conducted all business unanimously by 6-0 votes. Council approved the consent agenda 6-0 (with the 2017 annual crime report deferred to April 2) and held a public hearing on the upcoming FY 2018-19 budget and FY 2019-24 CIP (Item 15), where UE 150 city workers testified on aging, unsafe public works and water management trucks, flat $2,500 raises, $15/hour part-time pay, and arts compensation. Council then unanimously approved three development items in three 6-0 blocks: revisions to non-residential design commitments for Arringdon II (Item 16, 2 votes), a plan amendment and rezoning for 50 townhomes in Page Park II (Item 17, 3 votes), and a plan amendment and rezoning for a Volvo dealership at Park at South Point II (Item 18, 3 votes).

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence, Neighbor Spotlight, CROP Walk Proclamation, and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Charlie Reece moved and Council voted 6-0 to grant an excused absence to Mark-Anthony Middleton, who was stranded out of state by a broken airplane. Council presented the March Neighbor Spotlight to Constance Wright for Red Maple Park and proclaimed March 25 as Durham CROP Hunger Walk Day (in memory of Chuck Davis). After the City Manager noted Item 14 (2017 crime report) was deferred until April 2, Council approved the consent agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing on FY 2018-19 Budget and FY 2019-24 Capital Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened the pre-budget public hearing ahead of the May 21 budget presentation, June 4 hearing, and June 18 adoption. Six speakers addressed Council, including UE 150 stewards and city employees Daryl Brunson, Romy Gaddy, and Donald Quick—who cited aging 2003–2005 trucks breaking down in Water Management and Public Works, rising healthcare costs, merit-pay grievances, a demand for $2,500 across-the-board raises, and $15/hour pay for part-time and temporary workers—alongside artist Monica Byrne urging fair compensation for independent artists. No vote was taken.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to Design Commitments for Arringdon II (Z090015)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Jonathan Parsons' (J. Davis) request to clarify design commitment text for non-residential buildings and signs in the 95.6-acre Arringdon II mixed-use development east of Page Road without altering the overall development plan. Planning Commission recommended approval 10-0. Council adopted the consistency statement and zoning ordinance 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Item for Page Park II (4801 Crown Parkway, 50 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Stewart Inc.'s request on behalf of Lennar to amend the FLUM from Commercial to Low-Medium Density Residential and rezone Tract B at 4801 Crown Parkway to RSMD for 50 townhomes (priced around $200,000–$225,000) instead of 29,100 sq ft of retail (Planning Commission recommended approval 13-0). Javiera Caballero questioned BPAC's crosswalk and bike-lane comments (staff confirmed a crosswalk at site plan and an existing 14-foot outside lane), and Mayor Schewel noted the developer's DPS school proffer and urged builders to bring ideas on affordable housing. Council adopted all three motions 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for Park at South Point II (Southpoint Auto Park Boulevard)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jacob Wiggins presented Robert Schunk and attorney Ken Spaulding's request across nine parcels along Southpoint Auto Park Boulevard to amend the FLUM to Commercial and rezone to Commercial General with a development plan (CG(D)) for up to 55,000 sq ft of auto sales (a Volvo dealership), prohibiting outdoor paging systems and limiting impervious surface to 70% (Planning Commission approved 10-0). DeDreana Freeman questioned why landscaping standards differed from nearby Hendrick Southpoint, and staff agreed to provide a list of ordinance changes. Council adopted all three motions 6-0.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 8, 2018 City Council Work Session (presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel with six members answering roll call and DeDreana Freeman absent), Council unanimously approved a closed-session priority item for attorney-client consultation (6-0), settled the upcoming regular meeting agenda by voice vote, and voted unanimously to enter closed session. Mayor Schewel requested an administrative report on an Attorney General study indicating a high backlog of untested rape kits in Durham and praised the Holton construction job fair. During pulled-item discussions, staff explained per-household rapid rehousing costs ($8,000–$11,000) under a ~$320,000 Housing for New Hope contract targeting chronically homeless residents, while Finance Director David Boyd reviewed a projected $3.5 million positive General Fund variance, an $882,000 Debt Service Fund transfer to cover Parking Facilities debt, and scaling down a placeholder $150 million installment finance contract to roughly $98 million. Following a truncated middle section, Equal Opportunity/Equity Assurance Director Deborah Giles briefed Council on the 2016 Underutilized Business Enterprise (UBE) ordinance (using state/federal HUB, DOT, and SBA certifications and Good Faith Effort hearings) and the race- and gender-neutral Small Local Business Enterprise (SLBE) program for contracts under $500,000.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and City Attorney Closed-Session Priority Item
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the afternoon work session (following the three-hour morning affordable housing session) with six members answering roll call. He asked the City Manager for a report on an Attorney General study flagging a large number of untested rape kits in Durham and commended the Holton construction job fair. Council then voted 6-0 to approve the City Attorney's priority item for a post-meeting closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3).

agenda_items.title: Agenda Review, Housing for New Hope Rapid Rehousing Contract, and Q2 Financial / Debt Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council flagged items including the Housing for New Hope rapid rehousing contract and Item 3 (FY 2017-18 Q2 Financial Report). On Housing for New Hope, staff explained that ~$320,000 plus a $59,000 match would rehouse ~65 families, noting per-household costs ($8,000–$11,000 in 2016) rise when serving chronically homeless individuals with multiple barriers. Finance Director David Boyd confirmed a $3.5 million positive General Fund variance, explained an $882,000 annual Debt Service transfer supporting Parking Facilities debt, answered questions on CIP drainage projects and the $4.7 million failed-developments fund (Stonehill/Ravenstone), and clarified that Item 4's $150 million installment finance resolution is a placeholder scaled closer to $98 million.

agenda_items.title: Item 12: Equal Opportunity / Equity Assurance (UBE and SLBE Programs) Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming after a truncated middle section, EOEA Director Deborah Giles presented the legal framework and history of the 2013–2014 City-County Disparity Study and April 1, 2016 Underutilized Business Enterprise (UBE) ordinance, which eliminated separate city certification in favor of NC DOA HUB, NCDOT, and SBA certifications (expanding eligible firms from ~400 to ~3,000) and set categorical goals at 50% of market availability with Good Faith Effort hearings. She also explained the four-county race- and gender-neutral Small Local Business Enterprise (SLBE) program for informal construction ($500,000 or less) and A&E/surveying ($100,000 or less), noting SLBE does not preclude UBE goals on larger prime contracts. Council members asked why MBE goals exceeded WBE goals outside of goods and requested tracking metrics and networking dates.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Settlement and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council settled Consent Items 1–11, GBA Item 14, and GBA Public Hearings 15–18 by unanimous voice vote. Members then approved a motion by voice vote to enter closed session for attorney-client consultation under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) following a three-minute break.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting on Affordable Housing & Homelessness Support Services
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 8, 2018 Special City Council Meeting on Affordable Housing & Homelessness Support Services (presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel with all seven members present), Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented FY 2018-19 affordable housing goals and projected spending—including $2.9 million for Durham Housing Authority (DHA) partnerships rehabilitating 356 units across three properties, a $2.5 million multifamily rental production RFP, 230 rental/for-sale units, and 40+ owner-occupied repairs—while reviewing the 2016 five-year goals focused on households below 50% AMI amid roughly 11,000 severely cost-burdened Durham households. After a truncated middle section, staff presented the Focus Strategies homeless housing system assessment modeling expanded diversion and rapid rehousing, sparking a substantive policy debate over budget trade-offs between emergency shelters and the new strategy. Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton rejected a 'politics of scarcity' framing that would cut emergency shelter funding to pay for diversion and rapid rehousing, whereas an unnamed council member countered that finite budget resources require Council to pass additional funding if both shelter levels and the new strategy are to be maintained. No formal votes were taken; Mayor Schewel directed staff to return with concrete staged FY19 budget items and schedule a Joint City-County Committee presentation prior to adjourning at 1:01 PM.

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Strategy, FY 2018-19 Goals, and Five-Year Priorities Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the special meeting with all seven council members present, and Community Development Director Reginald Johnson outlined FY 2018-19 housing targets: first-phase financing for 356 DHA units across Damari, Morreene, and Laurel Oaks (plus downtown/Liberty), 230 new or preserved rental and for-sale units, 40+ owner-occupied repairs, $2.9 million projected for DHA, and a $2.5 million multifamily rental RFP. Reviewing data showing 11,000 severely cost-burdened households and 2,800 vouchers, Mayor Schewel invited discussion on whether to retain the 2016 five-year focus on <50% AMI given complaints from middle-income buyers priced out of West Durham and Northgate Park, while affirming he still supported targeting the greatest need alongside broader tools like the Jackson Street development (60% AMI with 20 units at 30% AMI).

agenda_items.title: Homeless Housing System Assessment (Focus Strategies) and Shelter vs. Rapid Rehousing Funding Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming after a truncated middle section, staff (Reginald Johnson and Sarah Zinn) walked through shelter intake at Urban Ministries and presented the Focus Strategies system assessment—launched in March 2017 with city/CoC funds and recently delivered to the Homeless Services Advisory Committee—recommending expanded diversion (mediation, case management, small rental/utility aid for singles and families) and rapid rehousing. During debate over funding priorities, Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed cutting emergency shelter budgets to fund the new strategy, while another member argued finite resources ('you can only spend it once') mean keeping shelters whole while funding diversion requires allocating additional budget dollars. Mayor Schewel asked staff to stage the homelessness plan with concrete FY19 budget requests and present it to the Joint City-County Committee before adjourning at 1:01 PM.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special City Council Meeting on Affordable Housing & Homelessness Support Services
disagreements.issue: Preserving Emergency Shelter Funding vs. Finite Budget Trade-Offs for Homelessness Diversion & Rapid Rehousing
disagreements.summary: Following the Focus Strategies homeless system assessment, Council debated whether expanding homelessness diversion and rapid rehousing should come from reallocating emergency shelter funds or from separate budget additions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Refuse to cut emergency shelter funding to pay for diversion and rapid rehousing; find cuts elsewhere or add dedicated funds.
side_a_arguments: Rejected a 'politics of scarcity' requiring cuts to emergency services that feed and shelter unhoused residents right now before the new strategy proves results.
Stated there are hundreds of other places in the city budget to cut before reducing emergency shelter support; another member echoed keeping shelters funded out of the broader budget.
disagreements.side_b_position: Recognize finite budget constraints ('you can only spend it once') requiring explicit Council budget action if both shelters and diversion are funded.
side_b_arguments: Noted that maintaining current shelter funding levels while expanding diversion and rapid rehousing is not a staff Community Development question but requires Council passing a budget with more total funding.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Steve Schewel affirmed supporting both shelters during the transition and the Focus Strategies plan, directing staff to bring staged FY19 budget items and schedule a Joint City-County presentation.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 5, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council met on March 5, 2018, issuing proclamations for Girl Scout Week and Women's History Month and swearing in inaugural members of the Mayor's Council for Women. Council approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 16) 7-0, adopting the Durham Sustainability Roadmap, transit vehicle replacements, and external auditor selection, and later approved pulled Item 16 (Spirit Communications telecommunications license) 7-0 after DeDreana Freeman commended the company for sharing workforce diversity statistics. Council unanimously approved 7-0 a consolidated annexation and rezoning for 79 townhomes at 5220 Wake Forest Highway (Item 19, 4 votes) and the permanent street closing of Rent Road for Ellis Road Phase II (Item 20). On Item 21 (NC 54 Storage at 1003 East NC Highway 54), Council unanimously approved the FLUM amendment and consistency statement 7-0 before passing the Commercial General zoning ordinance 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Vernetta Alston voting Aye and DeDreana Freeman voting Nay over downstream stormwater flooding concerns.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Consent Agenda Approval, and Swearing-In of Mayor's Council for Women
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Girl Scout Troop 998 and Cub Scout Troop 424 led the Pledge of Allegiance, followed by proclamations for Girl Scout Week and Women's History Month (honoring Jean Bradley Anderson). Council approved the consent agenda 7-0 (with Item 16 pulled by DeDreana Freeman for a brief question), adopting the Durham Sustainability Roadmap, transit radio and vehicle replacements, and external auditor selection, and then swore in inaugural members of the Mayor's Council for Women.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for 5220 Wake Forest Highway (79 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Eastwood Homes of Raleigh LLC's request for voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, FLUM amendment (Low to Low-Medium Density Residential), and rezoning to PDR 5.362 for up to 79 townhomes on 14.919 acres at 5220 Wake Forest Highway (Planning Commission approved 8-4). Commitments included a 50-foot southern setback, enhanced tree coverage, and bike-lane asphalt. Council adopted all four motions unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Rent Road Permanent Street Closing (896 Linear Feet)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Ellis Road Residential LP's request to permanently close 896 linear feet of Rent Road right-of-way to conform with the approved Ellis Road Phase II site plan (D1400380). Answering DeDreana Freeman's concern about converting public streets to private property without a fee, staff clarified that a new, realigned public road was replacing the closed segment. Council approved the street closing order 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Land Use Item for NC 54 Storage (1003 East NC Highway 54)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented a request to amend the FLUM from Office to Commercial and rezone 1.9 acres at 1003 East NC 54 from RS-20 to CG(D) for a 120,000-square-foot self-storage facility with a bus pull-out, bike-lane right-of-way, and cross-access easement (Planning Commission approved 8-4). DeDreana Freeman questioned Public Works staff Robert Joyner extensively about downstream stormwater runoff and potential flooding at nearby apartments, while Mayor Schewel suggested a stormwater facility tour for new council members. Council passed the FLUM amendment and consistency statement 7-0, and passed the zoning ordinance 6-1 with Freeman voting Nay.

agenda_items.title: Telecommunications License Agreement with Spirit Communications (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning to pulled Consent Item 16, DeDreana Freeman thanked South Carolina Telecommunications Group LLC (d/b/a Spirit Communications) for voluntarily sharing its workforce diversity statistics and engaging in constructive conversation on diversity as a small business. Council approved the telecommunications license agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Items 1–15 and 17, Excluding Pulled Item 16)
votes.discussion_detail: Approved consent agenda items including Mayor's Council for Women appointments, external auditor selection, transit upgrades, and Durham Sustainability Roadmap adoption.

votes.discussion_detail: Amended FLUM designation to Low-Medium Density Residential (4–8 du/acre).

votes.discussion_detail: Approved PDR 5.362 rezoning permitting up to 79 townhomes.

votes.discussion_detail: Approved closing 896 linear feet of Rent Road right-of-way to allow realignment under the approved Ellis Road Phase II site plan.

disagreements.issue: Downstream Stormwater Flooding Concerns on NC 54 Storage Rezoning (Item 21)
disagreements.summary: DeDreana Freeman cast the sole dissent (6-1) on the CG(D) zoning ordinance for NC 54 Storage after questioning whether stormwater detention elongation could worsen downstream flooding near neighboring apartments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the NC 54 Storage CG(D) rezoning relying on city stormwater detention and inspection standards
side_a_arguments: Public Works staff Robert Joyner explained stormwater impact analysis requires detention back to pre-development flow rates (up to 100-year storm events when downstream flooding exists)
Steve Schewel noted stormwater ponds are inspected annually and the city cannot ban uphill development solely on general proximity, proposing a stormwater tour for new members
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the CG(D) rezoning over downstream flooding risks to nearby apartments
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman expressed concern about observed flooding near the downstream apartments and potential impacts from elongated stormwater discharge
disagreements.resolution: FLUM and consistency motions passed 7-0, and the CG(D) rezoning ordinance passed 6-1.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 22, 2018 City Council Work Session presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel, the Council opened late after a morning closed session and unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items (revising motion language for external auditor selection and an asset management contract amendment, and scheduling a presentation on the Durham Sustainability Roadmap). Following a City Clerk supplemental priority item, Council unanimously voted to receive the item, suspend the rules, and appoint Casey Collins to the City-County Environmental Affairs Board after resolving an earlier February 5 agenda mix-up. Council reviewed consent items—highlighting MWBE subcontractor participation on waterline projects and praising the broad scope of the Sustainability Roadmap—and heard a Hope Valley Farms HOA speaker oppose reducing motor vehicle lanes on South Roxboro Street, referring the technical feedback to a March 7 public meeting. During the GoDurham Short-Range Transit Plan presentation, members debated transit equity and whether to reallocate funds from the fare-free Bull City Connector without Duke University financial support versus expanding fare-free access for low-income and vulnerable riders; Council then unanimously elected nine appointees to the Mayor's Commission on Women and settled the March 5 agenda (Consent Items 1–17, GBA Public Hearings Items 19–21).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and City Manager's Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the meeting late following a morning closed session and had the City Clerk call the roll, with members Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Vernetta Alston, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece called. The City Manager presented three priority items: modifying motion language and the agenda memo for external auditor selection to include the engagement letter and auditor's name, noting a presentation for Item 14 (Durham Sustainability Roadmap adoption), and revising motion language and the memo for Item 15 (Second Amendment to Asset Management Contract) following City Attorney review. Council approved the City Manager's priority items by unanimous voice vote.

agenda_items.title: City Clerk Priority Item: Environmental Affairs Board Appointment (Casey Collins)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk presented a supplemental priority item noting that at the January 18 work session, Casey Collins received four votes and Allison Blood received two votes on a ballot for an Environmental Affairs Board seat, but an error appeared on the February 5 Council agenda. Confirming both parties had been contacted and the issue resolved, the Clerk requested that Council suspend the rules and vote immediately to appoint Collins. Council passed three consecutive unanimous voice votes to receive the item, suspend the rules, and appoint Casey Collins.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After returning briefly to Announcements by Council (including lighthearted remarks about dual lapel microphones), Mayor Schewel read through administrative consent and general business items. Members pulled or flagged Item 5, Item 6 (Woodcroft Parkway extension municipal agreement), Item 13 (Cleveland Street parking lot lease for City employee parking), Item 14 (Durham Sustainability Roadmap presentation), Item 17 (Gordon Street Towns utility extension agreement), and Item 18 (GoDurham Short-Range Transit Plan presentation). On Items 9 and 10 (Central Park and West Main/North Elizabeth Street waterline contracts), a member praised strong minority and women-owned subcontractor participation (including 24% on Item 10) while noting none were Durham-based firms.

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matter: South Roxboro Street Lane Reduction Proposal (Hope Valley Farms HOA)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A representative of the Hope Valley Farms Homeowners Association reported that HOA members polled 3-to-1 against a proposal to reduce South Roxboro Street from two motor vehicle lanes in each direction to one lane in each direction. Citing National Association of City Transportation Officials (NACTO) standards, the speaker argued that narrowing vehicle lanes to 10 feet would curb speeding and leave enough width alongside the two-foot gutter for a bicycle lane without removing vehicle lanes. Mayor Schewel noted that staff had already replied by memo and encouraged residents to bring technical rebuttals to the scheduled March 7 public meeting.

agenda_items.title: External Auditor Selection Flag and Municipal Election Method Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A council member stated they had supported the external auditor item in the Audit Services Committee and would vote for it again, while flagging that the City was once again contracting with the same audit firm. At 00:19:18, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson revisited prior Council discussions on municipal election costs, noting that residents had opposed switching to a general-runoff system and the North Carolina General Assembly prohibits ranked-choice voting, while underscoring that holding two municipal elections incurs substantial unnecessary expense before the digest truncated.

agenda_items.title: Durham Sustainability Roadmap Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming near the conclusion of the presentation on Agenda Item 14 after a truncated middle section, a council member praised the Durham Sustainability Roadmap for broadening the City's definition of sustainability. The speaker highlighted how connecting areas such as the arts to sustainability expanded community understanding and expressed hope that residents would embrace that broader vision.

agenda_items.title: GoDurham Short-Range Transit Plan Presentation and Fare-Free Policy Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transit staff presented a cost-constrained Short-Range Transit Plan operating within the existing budget to address chronic route issues, add 9.3 miles of frequent service, and bring 12,700 more residents and jobs within 15-minute service and 16,000 more within 30-minute service (while identifying unfunded long-term needs such as later evening, Sunday, and Duke–North Durham cross-town service). Staff recommended reallocating resources away from the fare-free Bull City Connector (BCC) because it underperformed other routes. Council members questioned how fare-free routes were evaluated, cited ridership gains from free youth/student fares, debated whether the City should fund the BCC without Duke University support versus prioritizing vulnerable riders through passes or operator credits, and urged equitable transit access.

agenda_items.title: Appointments to the Mayor's Commission on Women, BPAC, and Citizens Advisory Committee
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following earlier discussion of the nine slots on the Mayor's Commission on Women, staff reported ballot tallies including Nida Allam and Gloria de Los Santos with six votes each and a tie at three votes, reading out the finalized nine-member slate across ward, public safety, and at-large positions (including Nana Asante-Smith, Megan McCurley, Ashley Kennedy, Mina Azigpe, Dolly Reeves, and Gloria de Los Santos). Council unanimously voted to elect all nine appointees to their respective slots. Near adjournment, the City Clerk also reported ballot tallies selecting Sean Mason (4 votes) for the Durham Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission and Sami Banawon (6 votes) for the Citizens Advisory Committee.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Unanimous voice vote on Mayor's Commission on Women slate)

agenda_items.title: Settling the Agenda for March 5, 2018 Council Meeting and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager presented the settled agenda for the upcoming regular meeting: Consent Items 1 through 17 and General Business Agenda (GBA) Public Hearings Items 19 through 21. Council approved the motion to settle the agenda by unanimous voice vote and adjourned.

votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous by Mayor Steve Schewel; mover, seconder, and individual roll-call votes were not recorded by name.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the City Manager's priority modifications to the external auditor selection motion/memo, Item 14 presentation notice, and Item 15 asset management contract amendment revisions.

votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous; mover, seconder, and individual voter names were not identified in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Received the City Clerk's late supplemental priority item regarding the Environmental Affairs Board energy seat appointment.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Vote on Environmental Affairs Board Appointment
votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous; mover, seconder, and individual voter names were not identified in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended Council rules to allow an immediate appointment vote at the work session to correct a February 5 Council agenda error.

votes.item_title: Appoint Casey Collins to the City-County Environmental Affairs Board
votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous; mover, seconder, and individual voter names were not identified in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Formally appointed Casey Collins, who had received four votes on the January 18 work session ballot compared to two votes for Allison Blood.

votes.item_title: Elect Nine Appointees to the Mayor's Commission on Women
votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous; mover, seconder, and individual voter names were not identified in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Elected the finalized nine-member slate into their designated ward, public safety, and at-large slots on the Mayor's Commission on Women following ballot tallying.

disagreements.issue: GoDurham Short-Range Transit Plan: Bull City Connector Reallocation vs. Fare-Free Transit Equity
disagreements.summary: During the GoDurham Short-Range Transit Plan briefing, staff recommended reallocating funds from the underperforming fare-free Bull City Connector (BCC), sparking council debate over how fare-free options were evaluated, Duke University's lack of financial support for the BCC, and equitable access for low-income and transit-dependent riders.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reallocate resources away from the underperforming Bull City Connector within the cost-constrained budget rather than subsidizing it without Duke support.
side_a_arguments: Transit staff noted the BCC underperforms other routes despite being fare-free and recommended shifting resources within the existing budget to expand 15-minute and 30-minute frequent service.

Council commentary questioned whether the City should continue funding the BCC as a free service without financial support from Duke University, especially after seeing ridership surge from making buses fare-free for students.
disagreements.side_b_position: Scrutinize the BCC cut, investigate alternative fare-free policies, and prioritize transit equity for vulnerable riders.
side_b_arguments: Council members questioned whether improvements to all-day service on the BCC had been adequately evaluated and why other fare-free route options were deemed unviable.

One speaker criticized the planning approach as inequitable, and Mark-Anthony Middleton urged solutions—such as bus operator discretion, credits, or passes for non-matriculating youth lacking school IDs—to serve the most vulnerable transit-dependent residents.
disagreements.resolution: Informational presentation and discussion only; no formal vote was taken on the Short-Range Transit Plan at the work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb 19, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council met on February 19, 2018 and conducted every vote unanimously 7-0. After approving the consent agenda 7-0 (including transit grant ordinances, Birchwood Park and American Tobacco Trail parking contracts, and a watershed protection plan), Council amended City Noise Ordinance Section 26-23 (Item 14) on a 7-0 motion by Charlie Reece to extend the Durham Central Park sound exception from 8:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. for groups such as Batalá Durham, before adopting the revised ordinance 7-0 and referring broader complaint-driven noise enforcement citywide to the Environmental Affairs Board. Council then unanimously adopted three Unified Development Ordinance text amendments in paired 7-0 consistency and ordinance votes: Omnibus 11 technical revisions (Item 10, TC170005), state-mandated sedimentation and erosion control updates (Item 11, TC170006, which Jillian Johnson criticized as General Assembly preemption weakening local environmental protections), and the landmark Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing Bonuses (Item 12, TC160005), granting administrative height, density (up to 75 units/acre), and zero-parking bonuses for transit-area projects reserving at least 15% of units for households at 60% AMI or below.

agenda_items.title: Pledge by Troop 451, Roll Call, and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel called the meeting to order, Troop 451 led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all seven council members were present. With no priority items, Council approved the consent agenda 7-0, covering the Cross Connection Control audit, transportation and Durham-Orange County transit grant ordinances, Birchwood Park and American Tobacco Trail parking construction, and South Ellerbe stormwater demolition.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City Noise Ordinance Section 26-23 (Durham Central Park)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney presented a noise ordinance amendment addressing complaints from Liberty Warehouse residents regarding rehearsals in Durham Central Park by the samba-reggae group Batalá Durham, proposing an exemption between 10:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. Batalá Durham representative Mr. Anderson welcomed clear rules and asked Council to consider other city parks as well, while Charlie Reece noted broader complaint-driven enforcement concerns were referred to the Environmental Affairs Board. Reece moved to extend the Central Park exemption window from 8:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m., which passed 7-0, followed by 7-0 adoption of the amended ordinance.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC170005 (Omnibus 11 Technical Revisions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Michael Stock presented Omnibus 11 (TC170005), containing technical corrections, reorganizations, and minor policy codifications across the UDO (recommended 13-0 by Planning Commission). With no public speakers, Council adopted the consistency statement and ordinance amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC170006 (Sedimentation, Erosion Control, and State Legislation)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Michael Stock presented TC170006 updating UDO subdivision exemptions, infrastructure performance guarantees, and sedimentation/erosion control rules to comply with North Carolina session laws (SL 2017-10, 2015-187, and 2017-40), approved 13-0 by Planning Commission. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Mayor Schewel noted for the public that state legislative preemption was forcing Durham to weaken local environmental and development protections. Council adopted both motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC160005: Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing Bonuses
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Hannah Jacobson presented TC160005 offering administrative density bonuses (up to 75 units/acre), height bonuses (up to 90 feet), and zero minimum parking in Compact Neighborhood light-rail transit tiers for walkable projects reserving at least 15% of units for households earning 60% AMI or less (tightened from 70% AMI average after work session feedback, consistent with Council's 2015 resolution). Affordable housing advocates praised linking zoning bonuses to 60% AMI affordability for the first time, while Council Member DeDreana Freeman and others discussed transit-station outreach and whether developers would utilize the bonuses. Council adopted the consistency statement and ordinance 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved amending Section 26-23(e)(7) to extend Durham Central Park's permitted sound window from 10:00 a.m.–8:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m.–9:00 p.m.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for TC170006.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 8, 2018 City Council Work Session presided over by Mayor Steve Schewel, the six present Council members unanimously excused absent Council Member Charlie Reece and reviewed consent, public hearing, and supplemental items for the upcoming regular meeting. Council received briefings on the South Ellerbe Stormwater Restoration building demolition contract, a police promotional testing and job task analysis contract for reclassified patrol and investigator ranks, and a Water Management watershed protection plan using roughly $100,000 annually from penny-per-tier water revenue in partnership with Triangle Land Conservancy. On a narrowly tailored City noise ordinance amendment drafted with absent Council Member Reece, members hesitated to approve piecemeal exceptions on city property without a broader policy review and favored waiting for Reece's return. Finally, City-County Planning staff led an extended work session review of the Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing UDO text amendment, sparking policy discussion over whether to set the density-bonus affordability target at 70% Area Median Income (AMI) for developer feasibility or adhere to the 60% AMI goal urged by the Planning Commission and housing advocates before settling the agenda unanimously (Consent 1–9 and 13; GBA 14; GBA Public Hearings 10–12).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Excusal of Council Member Charlie Reece, and Agenda Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel apologized for starting late and led roll call, noting that Council Member Charlie Reece was absent; Council approved a motion to excuse Reece by unanimous voice vote. After brief mention of an Environmental Affairs Board resolution, staff read the consent, public hearing, and supplemental items, pulling Item 5 (Watershed Protection Plan), Item 9 (South Ellerbe demolition contract), Item 12 (Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing UDO text amendment), Item 13 (Police promotional testing contract), and Item 14 (City noise ordinance amendment) for discussion.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Unanimous voice vote to excuse Reece)

agenda_items.title: South Ellerbe Stormwater Restoration Building Demolition Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In response to a council inquiry on Item 9, staff explained that the demolition contract removes above-ground structures while leaving building foundations in place until the next construction phase. Staff noted the demolition was accelerated ahead of broader construction and acknowledged council concerns that the interim site be kept safe.

agenda_items.title: Police Department Promotional Testing and Job Task Analysis Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police representative Kevin Gates answered council questions regarding the contract with Morris & McDaniel for promotional testing assessment services and job task analysis. Gates explained that because the department recently reclassified investigator and patrol officer positions as new ranks, it was applying the same formal promotional testing process used for other promotional ranks.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City Noise Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming mid-discussion on Item 14, staff noted that decibel limits are frequently exceeded across Durham and described the draft as a pared-down city-property exception developed with Council Member Charlie Reece. Members expressed concern about granting narrow piecemeal exceptions when the City had only made small tweaks to its noise ordinance over the past 20 years, discussed convening a stakeholder or community committee for a broader review, and noted willingness to hold the item until Reece returned. The item was placed on the General Business Agenda (GBA) rather than Consent.

agenda_items.title: Watershed Protection Plan and Conservation Easement Participation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Resources Planning Manager Sydney Miller and Water Management Director Don Greeley presented a formal framework to evaluate and fund watershed land conservation projects using approximately $100,000 per year generated by the 2011 'penny per tier' water rate structure. Adapting Raleigh's Upper Neuse Clean Water Initiative model with the Triangle Land Conservancy and a city-county technical and stakeholder team, the program enables Durham to partner on conservation easements where land trusts hold title and monitor properties protecting Durham's water supply.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment: Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City-County Planning staff presented proposed interim UDO regulations ahead of a public hearing in 10 days to advance the 2015 resolution and 2016 Comprehensive Plan policy calling for 15% of housing units within a half-mile of future transit station areas to be affordable. Staff proposed a 70% Area Median Income (AMI) average target (with units up to 80% AMI) to offer developer flexibility and help bridge the rental equity gap for by-right density and parking bonuses, while noting the Coalition for Affordable Housing and Transit and the Planning Commission recommended sticking to 60% AMI. Staff cautioned that short-term uptake would likely be limited where multifamily housing is permitted and that rental units above 60% AMI do not address Durham's deepest need, while noting Council could set the threshold at 60% and reassess within a year.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Placed on GBA Public Hearing)

agenda_items.title: Settling the Agenda and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager summarized the settled agenda for the February 19 Council meeting: Consent Items 1 through 9 and 13, GBA Item 14, and GBA Public Hearings Items 10 through 12. Council approved settling the agenda by unanimous voice vote and adjourned at 4:00 PM, noting a special Council meeting scheduled for March 8.

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member Charlie Reece from the Work Session
votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous among the six members present (Charlie Reece absent/excused); mover, seconder, and individual voter names were not recorded in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Steve Schewel noted Council Member Charlie Reece was absent and asked for a motion to excuse him.

disagreements.issue: Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing Target: 60% AMI vs. 70% AMI Average
disagreements.summary: During review of the Compact Neighborhood Interim Affordable Housing UDO text amendment, planning staff, the Planning Commission, the Coalition for Affordable Housing and Transit, and Council members weighed whether the by-right density bonus should set affordability at a 70% AMI average for financial viability or adhere strictly to the 2015 resolution's 60% AMI threshold.
disagreements.side_a_position: Use a 70% AMI average target (allowing units up to 80% AMI) to give developers flexibility and encourage use of the by-right density bonus.
side_a_arguments: Planning staff noted a significant equity gap between market rents and affordable rents near transit station areas and cited peer-city practice using a 70% AMI average.
Lowering the threshold to 60% AMI could reduce the effectiveness and developer uptake of the by-right incentive without substantial public subsidy.
disagreements.side_b_position: Adhere to the 60% AMI limit adopted in the 2015 City-County resolution and 2016 Comprehensive Plan.
side_b_arguments: The Coalition for Affordable Housing and Transit and the Planning Commission urged adhering to the letter of the 60% AMI resolution.
Discussion noted that rental units above 60% AMI do not address Durham's greatest housing need and that even at 60% AMI, Council could re-evaluate the ordinance's effectiveness after one year.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Item 12 was placed on the General Business Agenda for a public hearing in 10 days, with staff confirming the text could be amended to 60% AMI prior to the hearing if Council directed.

disagreements.issue: Noise Ordinance Amendment: Narrow City-Property Exception vs. Comprehensive Review
disagreements.summary: Council members expressed reservations about passing a narrow noise ordinance amendment drafted with absent Council Member Charlie Reece without undertaking a broader review of Durham's 20-year-old noise ordinance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pass the narrowly tailored city-property exception while planning a broader noise policy review.
side_a_arguments: Drafted as a pared-down, narrowly tailored exception limited to city properties because variances on private property are difficult to administer.
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay action until Council Member Charlie Reece returns and address noise policy more broadly through a stakeholder process.
side_b_arguments: Decibel limits are already exceeded regularly around Durham, making piecemeal exceptions problematic without comprehensive review.
Council Member Charlie Reece had led the drafting work and was absent, warranting waiting for his input and considering a community or stakeholder committee.
disagreements.resolution: Item 14 was placed on the General Business Agenda (not Consent) for the upcoming Council meeting with no vote taken at the work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb. 5, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: All seven members of the Durham City Council convened on February 5, 2018, opening with Mayor Steve Schewel's State of the City address—which highlighted participatory budgeting, $80 million in 2018 affordable housing investments, light-rail transit, police racial-equity reforms, and a food security coordinator—alongside a Human Relations Month proclamation. Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 13) 7-0, and approved both the Copley Farm rezoning for 123 residential units (Item 15, 2 votes) and the Angier Avenue consolidated annexation and rezoning for 78 single-family homes (Item 16, 3 votes) 7-0. On pulled Consent Item 13 (city code and fee revisions for small wireless 5G facilities under House Bill 310), Council split 4-3 to adopt the ordinance immediately over AT&T's request for a two-week delay: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved immediate adoption, while Steve Schewel explicitly announced he was voting Nay to grant a two-week delay and DeDreana Freeman voiced opposition regarding HB 310 preemption and delaying two weeks (individual names of the remaining voters were not read aloud on the record).

agenda_items.title: Mayor's State of the City Address, Neighbor Spotlight, and Human Relations Month Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel delivered his State of the City address outlining priorities including planning for participatory budgeting, $80 million in 2018 affordable housing efforts backed by Durham's dedicated two-cent housing tax levy, the $2.5 billion Durham-Orange Light Rail project, police reforms under Chief Davis (44% drop in car searches and misdemeanor diversion), and funding a food security coordinator. Council also presented a Neighbor Spotlight and proclaimed February 2018 as Human Relations Month honoring the Human Relations Commission's 50-year legacy.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Excluding Pulled Item 13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Item 13 (small wireless facilities) pulled for separate consideration, Council unanimously approved the consent agenda 7-0, including sidewalk construction administration contracts for Avondale and Campus Walk and a Campus Walk NCDOT supplemental agreement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change for Copley Farm (365 Freeman Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jacob Wiggins presented Lennar Homes' request to rezone 30 acres at 365 Freeman Road from Residential Rural to PDR 3.997 for up to 123 single-family, townhome, or semi-attached units with 24% maximum impervious surface (Planning Commission approved 13-0). Robert Schunk highlighted a $22,000 DPS school proffer and a Southern High School trades-program partnership, while Mayor Schewel urged developers to also develop affordable housing fund contributions for suburban developments. Council adopted the consistency statement and zoning ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation for Angier Avenue Residential (3838–3848 Angier Avenue)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Jamie Sunyak presented Angier Development LLC's voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, and rezoning from RS-20 and PDR 4.0 to PDR 3.958 for up to 78 single-family homes across 19.96 acres on Angier Avenue (Planning Commission approved 13-1). DeDreana Freeman commended developer David Lazo for holding a late-evening neighborhood meeting with residents. Council adopted the annexation, consistency statement, and zoning ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: City Code and Fee Ordinance Revisions for Small Wireless Facilities (Pulled from Consent)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: AT&T representative Robert Deroc requested a two-week delay on the small wireless (5G) ordinance to discuss potential discrepancies with NC House Bill 310 privately with staff. Public Works' Daniel Valero and the City Attorney confirmed the draft complied with HB 310 and noted permit applications were already arriving; Mark-Anthony Middleton rejected delaying for private offline talks after the work-session review, while DeDreana Freeman raised concerns over HB 310 pre-empting municipal right-of-way fees and Mayor Schewel favored granting a two-week grace period. Middleton moved immediate adoption, passing 4-3 with Mayor Schewel explicitly voting No on the record.

votes.item_title: Approve Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 13)
votes.discussion_detail: Approved consent agenda items including sidewalk engineering and construction inspection contracts.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for Copley Farm zoning case Z17.

votes.item_title: Item 15 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Amendment Rezoning Copley Farm from RR to PDR 3.997
votes.discussion_detail: Approved PDR 3.997 rezoning for up to 123 residential units at 365 Freeman Road.

votes.item_title: Item 16 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance and UEA for Angier Avenue Residential
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted voluntary annexation effective March 31, 2018 and utility extension agreement for 3838–3848 Angier Avenue.

votes.item_title: Item 16 (Motion 2): Adopt Consistency Statement for Angier Avenue Residential
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for Angier Avenue Residential.

votes.item_title: Item 16 (Motion 3): Adopt UDO Amendment Rezoning Angier Avenue Residential to PDR 3.958
votes.discussion_detail: Approved PDR 3.958 rezoning permitting up to 78 single-family homes along Angier Avenue.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Adopt City Code and Fee Ordinance Revisions for Small Wireless Facilities
votes.notes: Transcript announces 'Motion passes 4-3' without reading individual electronic votes aloud; Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and spoke in favor, Steve Schewel explicitly announced voting against, and DeDreana Freeman spoke critically of HB 310 and asked about a two-week delay.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved immediate adoption of the HB 310 small wireless facilities code and fee ordinance, while Steve Schewel announced his No vote to grant AT&T a two-week delay; motion passed 4-3.

disagreements.issue: Immediate Adoption vs. Two-Week Delay on Small Wireless Facilities (5G) Ordinance (Item 13)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on adopting the small wireless facilities code and fee ordinance immediately versus delaying two weeks after AT&T requested additional time to review House Bill 310 compliance with staff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the ordinance immediately and adjust later if needed
side_a_arguments: Public Works staff had already built the permit workflow and were actively receiving 5G small-cell applications without codified local authority
Mark-Anthony Middleton argued the item was vetted at work session, other utilities did not object, and Council should not pause for private offline negotiations
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay action two weeks for stakeholder feedback or oppose HB 310 restrictions
side_b_arguments: Steve Schewel voted No to grant AT&T two weeks of grace so utilities could review the published text
DeDreana Freeman questioned any harm from a two-week delay and raised concerns over HB 310 stripping municipal fee authority over public rights-of-way
disagreements.resolution: Ordinance passed 4-3, with City Manager Tom Bonfield and staff committing to meet with AT&T and bring back any needed amendments.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session - Rescheduled from January 18, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: At the rescheduled January 18, 2018 City Council Work Session, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson presided because Mayor Steve Schewel had to leave early, and Council welcomed newly appointed At-Large Council Member Javiera Caballero to her first work session. Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items—pulling Item 13 (small wireless facilities) for presentation, referring Item 14 (Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit planning) back to staff due to consultant travel constraints, and scheduling a snow-storm update—before hearing Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson's briefing on the city's 24-hour response to nearly 12 inches of Martin Luther King Jr. weekend snow, which exhausted the annual snow budget. Following a truncated middle section of the transcript covering public hearing items and Supplemental Item 17 (Commission on Confederate Monuments and Memorials), Council discussed Item 13 on state-mandated small-cell 5G wireless permitting in the public right-of-way, focusing on aesthetic controls, 300-foot pole spacing, and state preemption of local inspection fees. Council then unanimously settled the regular meeting agenda (Consent Items 1–13; GBA Public Hearings Items 15–16) and heard clerk ballot results naming Casey Collins (4 votes) for the Environmental Affairs Board and Carmen Nicole Williams (4 votes) for the Planning Commission before adjourning at 11:03 AM.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Welcome to Council Member Javiera Caballero, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson called the rescheduled work session to order at 10:00 AM and presided in place of Mayor Steve Schewel, who noted he had to depart early and would miss the first community conversation while attending the U.S. Conference of Mayors. Roll call noted Vernetta Alston as delayed while Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece were called; Council welcomed Caballero to her first work session and thanked staff for storm response. Council then unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items to pull Item 13 for presentation, refer Item 14 back to staff, and hear a snow-event briefing.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Unanimous voice vote on Manager's priority items)

agenda_items.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Weekend Snow Storm Response Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson briefed Council on the City's response to an unexpected 11-to-12-inch snow event initially forecast at 1 to 3 inches. More than 90 Public Works employees operated 40 trucks, loaders, backhoes, and motor graders in 24-hour shifts—clearing over 1,000 primary and 2,000 secondary/residential lane miles and depleting the annual snow budget—while 911 staff were housed in hotels, Group 1 Water Management staff stayed on 24-hour call with sewer cutoffs suspended, and operations coordinated every four to six hours with Joint City-County Emergency Management.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Review: Sidewalk Projects, Planning Items, and Confederate Monuments Commission
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff read agenda items including Avondale and Campus Walk Avenue South sidewalk contracts and NCDOT supplemental agreements (Items 9–12), small wireless facilities code revisions (Item 13), Coppley Farm 2 rezoning (Item 15), Andrew Avenue annexation (Item 16), and Supplemental Item 17 on the Commission on Confederate Monuments and Memorials. Council reordered the agenda to hear Item 17 first so Mayor Schewel could present before departing; discussion of those items occurred during a truncated portion of the transcript digest.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote recorded in transcript

agenda_items.title: City Code and Fee Ordinance Revisions for Small Wireless Facilities in the Right-of-Way
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming mid-presentation after the truncated section, staff and Assistant City Attorney Donald O'Toole explained proposed City Code permitting rules and fees driven by new North Carolina legislation (modeled on an AT&T sample ordinance) permitting 5G small-cell equipment on poles as close as 300 feet apart. Staff outlined benefits (reduced excavation) alongside drawbacks (aesthetics, construction disruption, new Development Services Center permitting workload, and potential conflicts with traffic poles), while noting that federal equal-access rules and 2016 state fee preemption restrict cost recovery to small fees such as $100 for the first facility. Council questioned data privacy/cybersecurity, unpermitted-work penalties, and license agreement termination enforcement.

agenda_items.title: Settling the Agenda, Board Ballot Results, and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously settled the regular meeting agenda with Consent Items 1 through 13 and GBA Public Hearings Items 15 and 16. The City Clerk announced ballot results selecting Casey Collins (4 votes) for the energy seat on the City-County Environmental Affairs Board and Carmen Nicole Williams (4 votes) for the Durham Planning Commission (term expiring June 30, 2020). After Council praised Spanish-language flyers advertising community budget conversations, Mayor Pro Tempore Johnson adjourned the meeting at 11:03 AM.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Unanimous voice vote to settle agenda)

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Voice vote declared unanimous by Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson; mover, seconder, and individual voter names were not identified in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved pulling Item 13 (small wireless facilities) for presentation, referring Item 14 (Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit planning) back to staff due to consultant travel constraints, and adding a snow-response briefing.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Jan 16, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: At its January 16, 2018 regular meeting, the Durham City Council seated newly appointed At-Large Council Member Javiera Caballero and honored retiring City Clerk D. Ann Gray with a proclamation and tributes recognizing her service and staff stability. Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (7-0), funding affordable housing awards for CASA and Durham Community Land Trustees, downtown wayfinding, employee benefits, a HIDTA grant amendment, sidewalk and street resurfacing contracts, and Esri software maintenance. Following an extensive public hearing on Item 12 (2101 House Avenue), Council voted unanimously 7-0 across three separate motions to amend the Future Land Use Map, adopt a consistency statement, and approve rezoning for a 78-unit multifamily project after the developer proffered reserving 50% of units for 10 years at 80% and 100% AMI for City, County, and Durham Public Schools employees. The meeting concluded with a non-agenda appeal from resident Barbara Lofton requesting assistance distributing space heaters to low-income seniors.

agenda_items.title: Seating and Remarks of Newly Appointed Council Member Javiera Caballero
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel invited newly appointed At-Large Council Member Javiera Caballero to take her seat on the dais and offer remarks. Council members noted that her formal appointment motion had been completed at the preceding special meeting and welcomed her to the council.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation and Retirement Tribute for City Clerk D. Ann Gray
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read a proclamation honoring retiring City Clerk D. Ann Gray for her long service to Durham. Council members praised her institutional knowledge, guidance at work sessions, and leadership of an office with virtually no staff turnover and strong customer service.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Affordable Housing Funds, Wayfinding, Employee Benefits, HIDTA Grant, Sidewalks & Streets, Esri)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the consent agenda, covering the 2017 municipal primary election, HOME CHDO funds for CASA (formerly Community Alternatives for Supportive Housing), dedicated housing and HOME CHDO funds for Durham Community Land Trustees projects on Kent Street, a downtown Durham Wayfinding Program grant agreement, 2018-2021 employee benefits recommendations, a 2016 HIDTA grant project ordinance amendment, 2018 sidewalk repairs (Contract SW-62) and street repaving (Contract ST-285), and an Esri software maintenance agreement. No items were pulled, and the consent slate was approved by electronic vote with newly seated Council Member Caballero participating.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Item for 2101 House Avenue (FLUM Amendment, Consistency Statement, and Zoning Map Change)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff (Jamie Sanyak) presented a Future Land Use Map amendment and rezoning for a 5.65-acre parcel at 2101 House Avenue to Residential Urban Multifamily with a development plan capping density at 78 units, resolving encroaching parking easements, and extending the Merrimack Street water line. Developer representative Dan Jule (for Broadmont Group) proffered reserving 25% of units at 80% AMI and 25% at 100% AMI for 10 years, with a 90-day pre-lease marketing period for City, County, and Durham Public Schools staff, drawing support from Phil Saab and Lizzie Ellis-Furlong (Durham Literacy Center). Opponent Lanier Blum questioned whether 80-100% AMI rents truly address low-income housing needs, criticized the lack of direct renter notification, and urged off-site sidewalks and relocating the driveway off Merrimack Street; Planning staff agreed to bring renter notification options to JCCC, and Council passed all three motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Non-Agenda Request: Heating Assistance for Durham Seniors (Barbara Lofton)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Barbara Lofton addressed Council regarding seniors lacking adequate winter heat and relying on unsafe heaters, requesting help from the city, churches, and residents to supply space heaters in coordination with the Durham Sheriff's Department. Council members thanked her for her advocacy on behalf of seniors and arranged to follow up after the meeting.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (2101 House Avenue): Future Land Use Map Amendment to Medium High Density Residential
votes.notes: First of three required motions for consolidated Item 12.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the public hearing and council discussion on workforce housing definitions, annual compliance monitoring, Merrimack Street traffic, off-site sidewalks, and renter notification procedures, Council closed the public hearing and moved to adopt the resolution amending the Comprehensive Plan Future Land Use Map from Medium Density Residential (6-12 units/acre) to Medium High Density Residential (8-20 units/acre). The motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (2101 House Avenue): Adoption of Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Second of three required motions for consolidated Item 12.
votes.discussion_detail: Council moved and seconded to adopt the consistency statement for the 2101 House Avenue rezoning request, passing unanimously 7-0.

votes.notes: Third of three required motions for consolidated Item 12; includes developer proffers (50% workforce units at 80%/100% AMI for 10 years, 90-day pre-lease period for public employees, and covered bike parking/pedestrian access).

meetings.title: Special Durham City Council Meeting Jan 10, 2018
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a special meeting on January 10, 2018 dedicated exclusively to hearing public testimony in support of the seven finalists for the vacant At-Large City Council seat. Mayor Steve Schewel established ground rules allocating 15 minutes of speaker time per candidate in alphabetical order, with bilingual Spanish-English interpretation provided and translation pauses excluded from each candidate's clock. Supporters addressed Council sequentially on behalf of finalists Shayla Arias, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, Karen Haldeman, Sheila Huggins, Carl Rist, and Pilar Rocha-Goldberg. No formal votes or council deliberations occurred, as Mayor Schewel reminded attendees that 45-minute candidate interviews would take place the following evening and the appointment vote would be held on January 16.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Process Ground Rules, and Bilingual Interpretation Setup
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel welcomed the seven finalists and members of the public, setting ground rules requiring positive advocacy without criticizing other candidates and granting each finalist 15 minutes for designated supporters to speak. Staff and interpreters Iris Ramirez and Jorge explained headset channels and live Spanish-English interpretation, with the City Clerk pausing the 15-minute clock during interpretation.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Shayla Arias
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters including Kim Swanson, Beth Messersmith, Jessica Burroughs, Tara Lemus, Jessica Berryman, and Yessenia Alvarez spoke on behalf of Shayla Arias. Speakers highlighted her journey as a naturalized citizen, her advocacy with MomsRising and Smart Start, her Latino community outreach nights on mental health and immigration resources, and her personal resilience.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Javiera Caballero
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters spoke in both English and Spanish on behalf of Javiera Caballero, emphasizing her experience as a teacher in Durham and her PTA presidency at Club Boulevard Elementary. Testimony praised her ability to stretch limited budgets, her partnership to bring Communities in Schools resources to students, and her ethical advocacy for immigrant and working families.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Pierce Freelon
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters including Chris Tiffany, Chris Massenburg, Angie Santiago, Jewel Taylor, Elizabeth Turnbull, George Roberson, Gabriel Eng-Goetz, and Michelle Gonzalez-Green spoke on behalf of Pierce Freelon. Speakers highlighted his independence from political action committees, his nonprofit youth leadership and fundraising work, and his advocacy on downtown gentrification.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Karen Haldeman
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers including Mayor Moss and Andrew Stillwell testified in support of Karen Haldeman. They cited her committee work, involvement with African American Heritage Day, strong communication skills, and collaborative encouragement of other candidates and women in civic life.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Sheila Huggins
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters spoke on behalf of Sheila Huggins, describing her grassroots neighborhood engagement in Northeast Central Durham, including Play Streets and Partners Against Crime meetings, as well as her broader civic organizing and advocacy across North Carolina.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Carl Rist
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel introduced the 15-minute public comment segment for finalist Carl Rist, during which supporters addressed Council regarding his qualifications for the vacant At-Large seat.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment in Support of Finalist Pilar Rocha-Goldberg
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Supporters including Sonia Rodriguez, Celestino Morales, Evan McDonald, and others testified in Spanish and English on behalf of Pilar Rocha-Goldberg. Speakers emphasized her eight years of nonprofit leadership, her wisdom and support for youth and families, and her deep roots in the community.

agenda_items.title: Closing Remarks and Appointment Schedule Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel thanked the Spanish interpreters, City Clerk staff, speakers, and all seven finalists, noting the difficulty of the council's upcoming choice. He reminded the public of the 45-minute candidate interviews scheduled for the following night at 5:00 p.m. and the appointment vote set for January 16 at 5:30 p.m., adjourning the meeting at 9:09 p.m.
